docs.title: Civex
docs.text: Civex keeps research data in order on your own computer: typed records, the files that belong to them, and workflows that process them. No cloud service and no database administrator are needed. Use it from the web app or the command line.

docs.title: Container plugins
docs.text:
Writing a plugin covers Tier 1: Python only, run via uv run as a subprocess. For a plugin that needs something the subprocess tier can't give — a different language, system binaries, GPU access, stricter resource limits — civex builds and runs it inside a Docker container instead: Tier 2. Both tiers speak the identical wire protocol — the same id/name/capabilities/Config/invoke() shape, the same frame types — over docker run -i <image> <mode> rather than a persistent subprocess.

Tier 2 is not wired into workflow execution yet

docs.title: The plugin directory
docs.text:
A container-tier plugin lives at _civex/plugins/<name>/, and is recognized as one (rather than a Tier 1 .py file) by the presence of both a civex-plugin.toml manifest and a Dockerfile in the same directory — that pairing is the whole marker; there's no separate registration step.

_civex/plugins/<name>/
  civex-plugin.toml   # id/name/category/capabilities manifest
  Dockerfile           # build context is this directory
  <source files>        # your plugin's implementation

docs.title: civex-plugin.toml
docs.text:
# Manifest for a Tier 2 (container) civex plugin. Lives alongside this
# plugin's Dockerfile and source in _civex/plugins/<name>/ -- the build
# context is this directory, so no separate path field is needed.

id = "my_project.my_container_plugin"  # must match Plugin.id in plugin.py
name = "My Container Plugin"
category = "transforms"
capabilities = []

id/name/category/capabilities here must stay in sync with whatever your plugin's own describe response declares — the manifest is what a container-tier registry could read without building and running the image; the describe response (produced by actually running the built image in describe mode) is the same information, once the image exists, and is what a plugin-authoring surface (CLI, UI, AI authoring guide) would read in practice.

docs.title: The Dockerfile
docs.text: The build context is the plugin's own directory — nothing outside it is visible to the build. Beyond that, it's an ordinary Dockerfile: install whatever runtime and dependencies your language needs, copy in your source, and set an ENTRYPOINT that ends up dispatching on sys.argv[1] / os.Args[1] / argv[1] (describe or run).

docs.title: The docker run -i <image> <mode> contract
docs.text:
The host runs your built image exactly like this — never anything more permissive:

echo '{"type":"describe"}' | docker run -i <image> describe
echo '{"type":"run","inputs":{...},"config":{...}}' | docker run -i <image> run

<mode> (the container's first argv) is describe or run. The container reads exactly one matching frame off stdin, does its work, writes exactly one response frame to stdout, and exits — one container process per operation, never a long-lived server. See Two dispatch models for why this differs from Tier 1's persistent process, and why it's actually useful here: a fresh container per call is what lets per-run --memory/--cpus limits and the timeout/kill wrapper apply cleanly to a single operation.

docs.title: Content-hash image caching
docs.text: Building a Docker image on every workflow run would be far too slow, so civex never does — ensure_image_built() (civex.plugins.container_build) hashes every file in the plugin's directory (Dockerfile, source, manifest, keyed by relative path so the hash doesn't depend on directory walk order) and tags the built image with that hash: civex-plugin-<safe-id>:<hash[:16]>. The tag is the cache key — an unchanged directory resolves to a tag docker image inspect already finds locally, so docker build is skipped entirely, and docker build never runs twice for the same contents. Edit any file in the plugin's directory and the hash (and therefore the tag) changes, so the next run builds fresh automatically. This is the same idea uv already applies to Python venvs, applied to Docker images instead.

docs.title: One worked example per language
docs.text: Every starter below implements the identical wire protocol — frame shapes, the describe/run dispatch on argv[1], and the fd-dup stdout-isolation trick from isolate_stdout() — so the host drives all of them with no per-language code.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Reuses civex-plugin-sdk directly — the same Plugin/Ctx classes Tier 1 uses, just served with serve_container() instead of serve():

templates/container-plugins/python/plugin.py
"""Starter template for a Tier 2 (container) civex plugin.

Rename `Plugin.id`/`name`/`category`, declare `capabilities`/`Config`, and
implement `invoke()` -- civex_plugin_sdk.serve_container handles the wire
protocol (frame parsing, the fd-dup stdout isolation trick, rpc_call
dispatch), the same SDK Tier 1 (subprocess) plugins use.

The host runs the built image as `docker run -i <image> describe` or
`docker run -i <image> run`; serve_container reads that mode from argv and,
for `run`, reads one `{"inputs": ..., "config": ...}` frame from stdin.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel

from civex_plugin_sdk import Ctx, Plugin, serve_container


class MyPlugin(Plugin):
    id = "my_project.my_container_plugin"  # must be unique; use a namespace prefix
    name = "My Container Plugin"
    category = "transforms"  # informational only
    capabilities: list[str] = []  # every ctx.* method this plugin calls

    class Config(BaseModel):
        pass

    def invoke(
        self, inputs: dict[str, Any], config: Config, ctx: Ctx
    ) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return {}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    serve_container(MyPlugin)

Starter: templates/container-plugins/python/.

docs.title: R
docs.text:
A hand-rolled shim (plugin.R, using jsonlite) implements the frame I/O and RPC round-trip directly; entrypoint.sh does the fd-dup isolation before Rscript starts, writing every protocol frame to /dev/fd/3 rather than through R's own stdout.

Starter: plugin-templates/r/.

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
Main.java speaks the protocol directly (id/name/capabilities/configSchema()/invoke()). Since Java has no portable dup2(), the stdout-isolation trick is done in entrypoint.sh instead of in-process — exec 3>&1; exec 1>/dev/null before the JVM starts — and Main writes frames through /proc/self/fd/3 rather than System.out.

Starter: plugin-templates/java/.

docs.title: Go
docs.text:
shim.go is the reusable protocol plumbing (frame I/O, the Ctx capability client, stdout isolation); main.go is the part you replace, implementing a small Plugin interface (ID/Name/Description/Category/Capabilities/ConfigSchema/Invoke).

Starter: templates/plugins/go/.

docs.title: Rust
docs.text:
Split into protocol.rs (frame shapes, mirroring civex_plugin_sdk.protocol), io.rs (fd-dup isolation + newline-delimited JSON I/O), ctx.rs (the Ctx capability client), and plugin.rs — the only file you edit, everything below its Shim plumbing marker stays as-is.

Starter: plugin-starters/rust/.

docs.title: C / C++
docs.text:
src/shim.c (protocol runtime: stdout isolation, frame I/O, describe/run dispatch, RPC calls) and src/json.c (a minimal dependency-free JSON value tree) are the plumbing; src/plugin.c is the example plugin you replace. Compiles with a C++ compiler unmodified, so a C++ plugin can reuse the same shim as-is.

Starter: starters/c/.

docs.title: SDK reference
docs.text: Generated from the docstrings in civex-plugin-sdk's public API (civex_plugin_sdk.__all__). See Writing a plugin for a guide to using it.

docs.title: civex_plugin_sdk
docs.text:
SDK for authoring out-of-process (subprocess/container tier) civex workflow plugins.

Subclass Plugin, declare id/name/inputs/outputs/Config, implement invoke(), and call serve() (Tier 1) or serve_container() (Tier 2) from the plugin script's __main__ -- see docs/extending/writing-a-plugin.md for the full authoring guide.

docs.title: IO_TYPES = ('any', 'string', 'number', 'boolean', 'bytes', 'table', 'files', 'records', 'mapping', 'list') module-attribute
docs.text:
Vocabulary for IOSpec.type.

Deliberately coarse: a step input/output is a live Python object (a DataFrame, raw bytes, a list of FileRef dicts), so this names the shape a workflow author needs to know when wiring one step into the next, not a validatable type. Nothing ever validates a runtime value against it -- host-side contract checking matches input and output names, never types.

any      no constraint / plugin-specific
string   text scalar
number   int or float
boolean  true/false
bytes    raw binary payload
table    tabular data (a pandas DataFrame in-process)
files    list of FileRef dicts ({sha256, filename, size})
records  list of record dicts
mapping  dict keyed by field/column name
list     list of anything not covered by files/records

docs.title: Plugin
docs.text:
Bases: PluginBase, ABC

Out-of-process plugin contract: PluginBase's declarative surface plus the one method that actually does the work.

Subclass this, set the PluginBase class attributes (id, name, inputs, outputs, Config, ...), and implement invoke(). Pass the subclass to civex_plugin_sdk.serve() (Tier 1) or serve_container() (Tier 2) -- nothing else needs to instantiate it.

docs.title: invoke(inputs, config, ctx) abstractmethod
docs.text:
Run this plugin for one workflow step.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default inputs dict[str, Any]

Step inputs, keyed by name, already converted from the wire form to invoke-time values (e.g. a declared table input arrives as a pandas DataFrame, not the wire envelope).

required config Any

An instance of this plugin's Config model, already validated against the run frame's config dict.

required ctx Ctx

The RPC-backed handle for reading/writing records, files, schemas, and collections beyond what inputs/config already supplied.

required

Returns:

Type Description dict[str, Any]

Step outputs, keyed by name, matching this plugin's declared

dict[str, Any]

outputs (when declared). Converted to the wire form

dict[str, Any]

automatically -- return a DataFrame or raw bytes directly for a

dict[str, Any]

table/bytes output.

docs.title: PluginBase
docs.text:
Declarative metadata shared by every plugin tier (BUILTIN, SUBPROCESS, CONTAINER).

Set the class attributes below on a subclass; invoke() itself is declared separately by each tier (see this package's Plugin for the out-of-process one).

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
Bases: BaseModel

A plugin's run-time configuration.

Override with the fields this plugin actually accepts; the model is rendered to JSON Schema for describe and validated against the run frame's config dict before invoke() is called.

docs.title: IOSpec
docs.text:
Bases: BaseModel

One declared input or output of a plugin.

type is a plain str rather than a Literal[IO_TYPES] on purpose: this model crosses the wire in a describe_result, and a Literal would make an older host fail discovery entirely on a plugin built against a newer SDK that added a vocabulary entry. An unrecognized type should degrade to being displayed as-is, not take the plugin down. In-repo declarations are held to the vocabulary by test, where a typo is worth failing on.

docs.title: Ctx
docs.text:
The handle invoke() receives for everything beyond inputs/config: records, files, schemas, and collections.

Every method blocks on a single rpc_call/rpc_result round trip over writer/reader -- there is no batching or concurrency, so a plugin calling several Ctx methods pays one blocking round trip per call.

docs.title: run_dir property
docs.text: The run's folder, where a plugin may write files to store_path (None from an older host).

docs.title: progress(done, total=None, message='')
docs.text:
Say how far this run has got, for whoever is watching it.

The civex app shows it in the status bar while the run lasts. Cheap (one line to the host, no answer), but there is no point in calling it more than a few times a second.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default done float

How much is done (items, bytes, ...).

required total float | None

How much there is in all, or None if unknown.

None message str

What it is doing now, e.g. "Reading sel_03.txt".

''

docs.title: get_context_record()
docs.text:
Return the record that triggered this workflow step.

Ctx has no ambient .record/.dataset fields the way in-process WorkflowContext does -- this (and get_context_dataset()) is the only way an out-of-process plugin learns what triggered it.

docs.title: get_context_dataset()
docs.text: Return the dataset that owns get_context_record()'s record.

docs.title: get_file(sha256)
docs.text: Return the raw bytes stored under sha256 in the object store.

docs.title: file_path(sha256)
docs.text:
Return a path to a read-only copy of a stored file, in the run's folder.

Prefer this to get_file for anything large: nothing is read into memory or sent over the protocol. The copy is removed when the run ends. Needs read (protocol 3).

docs.title: store_path(path, filename)
docs.text:
Store the file at path (which must be in the run's folder: run_dir) and return its FileRef dict.

Prefer this to store_file for anything large: the host reads the file itself. Needs manage_files (protocol 3).

docs.title: store_file(data, filename)
docs.text: Write data to the object store and return its FileRef dict ({sha256, filename, size}).

docs.title: update_record(record_id, data)
docs.text:
Replace the values of the record identified by record_id with data and return it.

Fields not in data are cleared; to change only some fields use patch_record. Needs write_records.

docs.title: create_record(dataset_name, schema_name, data, context_record_id=None)
docs.text:
Create a record in dataset_name against schema_name and return it.

context_record_id, when omitted, defaults host-side to get_context_record()'s id -- see WorkflowContext.create_record's docstring for why it isn't called parent_record_id.

docs.title: patch_record(record_id, fields)
docs.text:
Change only fields of a record and return it; every other field stays as it is now.

Prefer this to update_record, which replaces the record's whole data with what it is given (so fields left out are cleared). Nothing is written, and nothing is triggered, when the fields already hold these values. Needs write_records.

docs.title: get_record(record_id)
docs.text: Return the record identified by record_id.

docs.title: commit()
docs.text:
Do nothing (deprecated).

A run's writes are kept or dropped whole when it ends: civex keeps them if every step succeeds and undoes them all if one fails, so a plugin no longer commits part of a run. Kept so plugins that call it still run; it sends nothing.

docs.title: PluginError
docs.text:
Bases: Exception

Base class for every error this SDK raises. Carries the {kind, message, retryable} envelope this module documents above.

Raise this directly (with a custom kind) from invoke() for a failure that doesn't fit one of the more specific subclasses below.

docs.title: to_envelope()
docs.text: Return the {kind, message, retryable} dict this error sends over the wire.

docs.title: CapabilityDeniedError
docs.text:
Bases: PluginError

Raised host-side when a plugin issues an rpc_call for a method it didn't declare in its describe capabilities list.

docs.title: ConfigValidationError
docs.text:
Bases: PluginError

Raised when incoming run config fails validation against the plugin's declared Config model.

docs.title: RpcError
docs.text:
Bases: PluginError

Raised plugin-side when the host responds to an rpc_call with an error frame.

docs.title: serve_container(plugin_cls)
docs.text:
Container-tier entrypoint: isolates the actual stdout fd, then performs exactly one describe or run (per sys.argv[1]) off real stdin.

Call this (and only this) from a container-tier plugin's main -- see docs/extending/container-plugins.md.

docs.title: serve(plugin_cls)
docs.text:
Real entrypoint: isolates the actual stdout fd, then serves forever off real stdin.

Call this (and only this) from a plugin's main.

docs.title: The wire protocol
docs.text:
This is the reference writing a plugin and container plugins both build on, and what makes it possible to write a plugin in a language the civex SDK doesn't exist for — a new-language starter only has to implement these frame shapes, not link against any civex code.

Newline-delimited JSON: one JSON object per line, in both directions over a single stdin/stdout pair — no length prefix. The host and the plugin process take turns; the protocol is strictly synchronous with no interleaving, so a blocking read for the next line is always sufficient on either side.

docs.title: Frame types
docs.text:
Every frame has a "type" field naming which of the following it is.

Host → plugin

Type Purpose describe "Tell me your contract." Carries no fields; the plugin responds with describe_result. run Run one workflow step: {"type":"run","inputs":{...},"config":{...}}. rpc_result The successful response to a plugin's rpc_call, matched by call_id: {"type":"rpc_result","call_id":"...","result":{...}}. error An rpc_call failed. Carries the same error envelope shape the plugin uses for its own failures.

Plugin → host

Type Purpose describe_result The plugin's complete contract: id, name, description, category, capabilities, inputs/outputs, config_schema. Identical in shape for every tier, so no consumer (CLI plugin info, GET /plugins, the frontend plugin panel, the AI authoring guide) needs a per-tier branch. result invoke() succeeded: {"type":"result","outputs":{...}}. error A run (or rpc_call) failed: {"type":"error","call_id":null,"error":{"kind":...,"message":...,"retryable":...}}. call_id is set when this is a response to a specific rpc_call, unset for a top-level run failure. log A line the plugin printed: {"type":"log","stream":"stdout","text":"..."}. The host writes it to the run's log. No answer. progress How far the current run has got: {"type":"progress","done":3,"total":12,"message":"Reading sel_03.txt"} (total may be null). The app shows it in the status bar while the run lasts. No answer. Protocol 2. rpc_call Invoke one RPC method, blocking for the matching rpc_result/error: {"type":"rpc_call","call_id":"...","method":"...","params":{...}}.

error is genuinely bidirectional — the host sends it in response to a failed rpc_call, the plugin sends it in response to a failed describe/run or to report an RPC failure it can't otherwise express. Both directions share the one ErrorFrame shape.

docs.title: How a plugin is started
docs.text:
Every plugin speaks identical frames; only how it is started differs, and that is all a tier is in civex (a launcher, civex.plugins.launchers). The host drives every one the same way (civex.plugins.runtime).

Built-in — a thread in civex. civex's own plugins are SDK Plugins served by serve_loop on a thread of civex's process, over in-memory streams of the same JSON frames, kept between runs like a subprocess. Trusted code: not stopped by a step's timeout.

Tier 1 (subprocess) — persistent process. The host spawns uv run --no-project <plugin>.py once and keeps it alive across runs: the same process answers the describe at discovery and every later run of that plugin, until it has been idle for a while (civex.plugins.workers). A process that timed out, died or sent a malformed frame is stopped instead of reused. The plugin loops reading frames off real stdin, dispatching on each one's type (describe or run), and can be asked to describe itself and then run in the same process lifetime. This is civex_plugin_sdk.serve() (serve_loop internally).

Tier 2 (container) — one process per operation. The host runs docker run -i <image> <mode>, where <mode> is describe or run, passed as sys.argv[1] rather than inferred from the first frame — a fresh container per call is what lets per-run --memory/--cpus limits and the timeout/kill wrapper apply per operation rather than for the container's whole lifetime. The plugin reads exactly one frame (matching the requested mode) and exits. This is civex_plugin_sdk.serve_container() (serve_container_once internally) — same frame parsing, same RPC dispatch, same stdout isolation as Tier 1, just single-shot instead of looping.

docs.title: isolate_stdout(): keeping stray output off the wire
docs.text:
Before any plugin code runs, the SDK duplicates the real stdout file descriptor (fd 1) to a private fd, then redirects the public fd 1 to /dev/null. Every protocol frame is written through that private duped fd (FrameWriter), never through the public one, so output can never interleave with, or corrupt, the JSON on the wire.

sys.stdout is then replaced by a LogStream, which sends each line written to it as a log frame: a print() from your plugin reaches the run's log, in order with the run's other frames (a half-printed line is sent before the run's answer). Only output written straight to fd 1 by C code is lost. Anything written to stderr (warnings, the logging module's default handler, a traceback) is read by the host as it comes and also goes to the run's log; the last lines of it are kept for the message when a plugin process dies.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
describe_result carries the protocol_version the plugin's SDK speaks (absent means 1). The host runs a plugin whose version is anywhere from 1 to its own, since each version so far only added what a plugin may send; it refuses a newer one with a message saying to update civex.

Version Change 1 The frames above, less progress. 2 progress frames. 3 run names the run's folder (run_dir); host functions file_path and store_path.

docs.title: Binary payloads: inline or a file in the run's folder
docs.text: Small bytes values cross inline as base64. Each run names the run's folder (run_dir, protocol 3), shared by every step of a workflow run and removed when it ends: a value above the inline threshold is written there and the frame carries its path, and the files a plugin asks for (get_file, file_path) are copied there (read-only copies, never links to what is stored) and handed over by path. A container gets the folder mounted at the same path. Every path a plugin sends back (a value in its answer, a file to store) must be inside the run's folder or its own working folder; civex refuses any other (path_refused), since the next step may run inside civex and read what the path names.

docs.title: table and bytes on the wire
docs.text:
Declared table/bytes IOSpec values cross the wire through one shared conversion (civex_plugin_sdk.io_convert), used identically by every tier so a plugin author's code never has to know or care which one it's running under:

  • bytes crosses as the same inline-or-scratch-path envelope described above.
  • table crosses as columnar, typed records: {"encoding": "inline", "columns": [...], "dtypes": {col: civex_type}, "data": {col: [values...]}} when small, or {"encoding": "ndjson_path", "path": "..."} above a row-count threshold (one JSON row object per line, first line a {"columns": ..., "dtypes": ...} header) — so a step that's merely relaying a table between two other steps never has to hold or embed the full contents, only whichever step actually reads it does. dtypes reuses civex's own scalar field vocabulary (integer/float/string/boolean/date/datetime), not a pandas-specific one, so a table means the same thing here as everywhere else in civex and round-trips through non-Python tiers with no pandas-specific knowledge required on their end.

A Python plugin author never sees either envelope directly — a table input arrives as a real pandas DataFrame, a bytes input as real bytes; the SDK converts back to the wire form on the way out.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
A plugin declares what it needs via its capabilities list, returned as part of describe_result. That list is captured once, at discovery time — when the host first spawns the plugin to ask it to describe itself — and is what gets passed into run_plugin(...)/run_container(...) for every subsequent run. It is never re-derived from the live process making the RPC calls: a plugin that declared a narrow capabilities list at discovery but tries to call something wider at run time is exactly the case this is meant to catch, and it fails with a capability_denied error rather than being silently permitted because the running process asked nicely.

RPC methods on the wire are get_file, update_record, create_record, commit, plus one generic call_tool that carries every other host function (get_context_record, find_records, patch_record, store_file, ...) without a protocol change — call_tool's params are always {"tool": <name>, "args": {...}}. On the host a method and a tool are the same thing: a name in one table of host functions (civex.plugins.host_api), each needing a permission action. A plugin's capabilities list those actions (read, write_records, manage_files, delete), or, in the older form, single function names; the host works out once, at discovery, which functions that grants, and refuses any other with capability_denied. commit is answered and does nothing: the host keeps a run's writes when it ends, or none of them if a step failed.

Built-in plugins are held to the same rule. They are SDK Plugins too, run in civex's own process by the SDK's serve_loop on a thread, over in-memory streams carrying the same JSON frames (civex.plugins.launchers.InProcessLauncher), so a built-in reaches the project only through the host functions its capabilities grant, exactly as a plugin in a process does. Unlike one, it isn't stopped by a step's timeout: a thread can't be killed.

docs.title: Writing a plugin
docs.text:
You can extend civex with your own plugins. Place a .py file in _civex/plugins/ and civex discovers it automatically — no registration required.

Custom plugins run as real, isolated OS processes (uv run --no-project <plugin>.py), not imported into civex's own process. Each run gets its own dependency environment (declared inline in the file — no editing civex's own pyproject.toml, ever), its own process group (killed as a unit if it exceeds its timeout), a throwaway working directory with no ambient path into your project data, and access to project data only through the RPC calls it explicitly declares.

This is the Tier 1 (subprocess) path — Python only, run via uv run. If you need a different language, system binaries, GPU access, or stricter resource limits, see Container plugins instead. Both tiers speak the same wire protocol.

docs.title: Minimal example
docs.text:
civex-plugin-sdk/examples/echo_plugin.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10"
# dependencies = ["civex-plugin-sdk"]
# ///
"""Minimal reference plugin exercising the full protocol surface: describe,
run, config validation, and one rpc_call (update_record) when asked to.

In a real subprocess-tier deployment this file is invoked via
`uv run --script echo_plugin.py`, which resolves `civex-plugin-sdk` from the
PEP 723 header above with no manual environment setup. This repo's own
tests invoke it directly (the SDK is already on the path via the uv
workspace venv) to exercise the wire protocol over a real subprocess
boundary without needing a published package.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any

from pydantic import BaseModel

from civex_plugin_sdk import Ctx, Plugin, serve


class EchoPlugin(Plugin):
    id = "example.echo"
    name = "Echo"
    category = "example"
    capabilities = ["write_records"]

    class Config(BaseModel):
        text: str

    def invoke(
        self, inputs: dict[str, Any], config: Config, ctx: Ctx
    ) -> dict[str, Any]:
        if inputs.get("call_host"):
            ctx.update_record("r1", {})
        return {"echo": config.text, "inputs": inputs}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    serve(EchoPlugin)

Use it in a workflow:

- id: compute
  plugin: example.echo
  config:
    text: hello
  timeout: 30   # optional; overrides [plugins].default_timeout_seconds from config.toml

- id: save
  plugin: civex.set_fields@1
  config:
    field: greeting
  inputs:
    value: compute.echo

Which SDK version does my plugin get?

civex-plugin-sdk is a normal PyPI package (MIT licensed), so the plain dependencies = ["civex-plugin-sdk"] line resolves like any other. When civex first starts your plugin it locks its dependencies (uv lock --script, a <plugin>.py.lock file beside it), and from then on runs exactly those versions, without asking a package index, until you change the dependencies. Updating civex doesn't rebuild the plugin's environment: civex speaks every wire protocol version from 1 to its own, and refuses a plugin on a newer one with a message saying which side to upgrade. Delete the lockfile to take newer versions.

docs.title: The header: what civex knows without running the plugin
docs.text:
When you save a plugin from the app (or run civex plugin check --write <plugin>.py), civex asks it once what it is and writes the answer into the script block at the top of the file, under [tool.civex]: its id, name, capabilities, inputs, outputs and config schema. From then on civex knows the plugin by reading that, without running it (discovery, the workflow checks, the shared library). Don't edit it by hand: change the code and save again.

When the plugin's process starts, civex asks the code again, and refuses to run a plugin whose code no longer says what its header does (it asks for a capability the header doesn't grant, say) until the header is written again from the code. civex plugin check <plugin>.py says whether they agree. A plugin with no header is described by running it, as before.

docs.title: Plugin structure
docs.text:
Every plugin file must:

  1. Start with a PEP 723 inline script metadata block declaring civex-plugin-sdk as a dependency (plus anything else the plugin needs — pandas, requests, whatever). uv run resolves and caches an isolated venv for it automatically, the first time it's used, and civex locks what it resolved (see above). civex adds the [tool.civex] header to this block when you save.
  2. Define a class subclassing the SDK's Plugin ABC (import it directly, or under an alias like Plugin as PluginBase if you want to name your own subclass Plugin too).
  3. Call serve(YourPluginClass) inside if __name__ == "__main__":.
Attribute Type Description id string Unique identifier used in workflow YAML. Prefix with your project name to avoid collisions. name string Human-readable name shown in the UI. category string Informational grouping. No functional effect. capabilities list[string] The permission actions the plugin needs ("read", "write_records", "manage_files", "delete"; see The Ctx API). A call it wasn't granted fails at run time with a capability_denied error — the host enforces this against the list your plugin declared at discovery time, not anything the running process claims about itself. See Capabilities for how this is enforced on the wire.

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
Declare a Config class that inherits from pydantic.BaseModel. Its fields become the keys in the step's config: block. Pydantic handles type coercion and validation automatically — validated for real inside your plugin's own process, not just checked against a JSON schema at save time.

class Config(BaseModel):
    field: str
    multiplier: float = 1.0         # optional with default
    mode: str = "linear"

docs.title: How the workflow builder shows a setting
docs.text:
The workflow builder makes a form from your Config: each setting's title is its label and its description goes in a tooltip. By default a setting gets a plain text, number, checkbox or list box. To get a better control, say what the setting is with an x-civex entry in its JSON schema:

from pydantic import Field

class Config(BaseModel):
    field: str = Field(
        title="Field with the recording",
        json_schema_extra={"x-civex": {"kind": "field", "dtypes": ["file"]}},
    )
    method: str = Field(
        "fast",
        title="Method",
        json_schema_extra={"x-civex": {"kind": "choice", "choices": [
            {"value": "fast", "label": "Fast"},
            {"value": "exact", "label": "Exact"},
        ]}},
    )
kind Control Other keys field A list of the fields of the record the workflow runs on of: the setting that holds a schema, to list that schema's fields instead; dtypes: the field types to list schema A list of schemas collection A list of collections (blank: the record's own) record A record id (blank: the record the workflow runs on) choice A list of choices ({value, label}) pattern A regular expression with one capture group, with Build from an example…, which writes it from a file name the person marks on: field (the names of the files in the setting called field) or files (files given when it is run); date_format: the setting a date in the name fills; read_as: the setting saying what the value is read as (string, integer, date, …); keys: true when the value is matched against records, so names giving the same key are shown date_format A token format such as YYYYMMDD-HHmmSS pattern: the pattern setting it goes with

Add "advanced": true to put a setting under More settings. Nothing is checked from these hints: they only choose the control, and a setting without one still works.

The builder and a workflow's Overview also say what each step does in one sentence. Give it on the Config model with says(), naming settings and inputs in braces; each is filled in with what the person chose, by its name in the app ("Recorded on", not recorded_on), and shows as "…" until chosen:

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
from civex.plugins.hints import says

class Config(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(
        json_schema_extra=says("Measures the pitch of the recording in {field}.")
    )

The sentence is stored as x-civex-says in the JSON schema. Write it the way a person would describe the step to a colleague, and write each input's and output's description the same way: the builder labels an input by the first clause of its description ("The files to put on records." becomes Files to put on records) and an earlier step's output by its description ("Step 1: the file's contents").

docs.title: invoke()
docs.text:
def invoke(
    self,
    inputs: dict,   # values from input references
    config: Config,  # validated config from the workflow YAML
    ctx: Ctx,        # RPC client for the capabilities you declared
) -> dict:
    ...
    return {"output_name": value}

Return a dict of output values. These are referenced by downstream steps as this_step_id.output_name. Return an empty dict {} if the step produces no outputs.

Warning

If invoke() raises, the whole workflow job is marked failed and no changes made by earlier steps in the same run are committed (the executor commits once, at the end, after every step succeeds).

docs.title: The Ctx API
docs.text:
Ctx is deliberately more restrictive than a plain in-process object: it has no ambient .record/.dataset — a plugin can't accidentally read anything it wasn't granted. Everything goes over an RPC call to the host, checked against what the plugin's capabilities grant before it runs.

Capabilities are permission actions. List the ones your plugin needs; each grants every method in its row below. (Naming a single method instead, capabilities = ["find_records"], grants just that one: the older form, still read.) Whatever is granted, the call is also held to what the person running the workflow may do in the project.

Needs Methods read ctx.get_context_record() (the record the run is for: id, schema_id, data, ...; the only way to learn it), ctx.get_context_dataset() (its collection), ctx.get_record(record_id), ctx.find_records(dataset_name, schema_name=None, parent_record_id=None, filters=None, search=None, limit=50, offset=0), ctx.get_file(sha256) (a stored file's bytes), ctx.file_path(sha256) (a read-only copy of a stored file in the run's folder, as a path: nothing read into memory; use this for large files), ctx.get_schema(name), ctx.list_schemas(), ctx.get_collection(name), ctx.list_collections() write_records ctx.patch_record(record_id, fields) (change only these fields; writes nothing when they already hold these values: use this), ctx.update_record(record_id, data) (replaces the record's data: fields left out are cleared), ctx.create_record(dataset_name, schema_name, data, context_record_id=None) (inside the run's record unless told otherwise; triggers fire for it as usual) manage_files ctx.store_file(data, filename) (store bytes in the run's collection; returns a FileRef-shaped dict), ctx.store_path(path, filename) (store a file you wrote in the run's folder, ctx.run_dir; read by civex itself, so large files never pass through the protocol) delete ctx.delete_record(record_id) (it can be restored from Activity)

These need nothing, since they read and change nothing of the project's:

Method Description ctx.progress(done, total=None, message="") Say how far the run has got ("Reading sel_03.txt", 3 of 12). The app shows it in the status bar while the run lasts. print(...) Goes to the run's log (see the run's page), as does anything written to stderr.

There is no commit. A run's writes are kept when every step succeeds and all undone if one fails, so a failed run never leaves records half-changed. (ctx.commit() still exists for plugins written before, and does nothing.)

See the SDK reference for the full generated API, including exact signatures and return types.

docs.title: Reading and writing the trigger record
docs.text:
record = ctx.get_context_record()
value = record["data"].get("reading")   # None if not set

ctx.patch_record(record["id"], {"duration": 42.5})   # only this field changes

Or use civex.set_fields@1 as a separate workflow step instead of calling ctx.update_record directly.

docs.title: The run's folder
docs.text: Each workflow run has a folder of its own, removed when the run ends (ctx.run_dir). The files a plugin asks for (ctx.file_path, ctx.get_file) are copied there, and any table or bytes value too large to send inline is written there, so a later step can read what an earlier one wrote. A plugin may hand back only files inside that folder (or its own working folder): civex refuses a path anywhere else (path_refused).

docs.title: Accessing files
docs.text:
record = ctx.get_context_record()
ref = record["data"].get("reading")   # {"sha256": "...", "filename": "...", "size": ...}
if ref:
    raw_bytes = ctx.get_file(ref["sha256"])

docs.title: Isolation and timeouts
docs.text:
• A plugin runs as a uv run --no-project subprocess with its own process group, killed as a unit (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL if it doesn't exit) if it exceeds its timeout.
  • The process is kept between runs: once started (or asked to describe itself), it answers the next run of the same plugin too, until it has been idle for five minutes or civex stops. Editing the file starts a new one. So module-level state in your plugin lives from one run to the next; anything a run must not see from the last belongs inside invoke(). A process that times out or dies is not reused.
  • Default timeout is [plugins].default_timeout_seconds in _civex/config.toml (60s if unset); override per step with timeout: <seconds> on the workflow step.
  • The subprocess's working directory is a throwaway scratch dir, emptied before each run, never your project's _civex/ — a plugin has no ambient filesystem path into real project data, only what it fetches over the ctx.* capability calls it declared.
  • The subprocess's environment is minimal (PATH, HOME, a few uv/Python variables) — it can't read civex's own environment (database URL, AI API keys, ...).

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• Plugins run as separate OS processes, not imported into civex's own process — they never import civex.* modules directly, only civex_plugin_sdk.
  • A plugin can only reach project data through the ctx.* calls it declared in capabilities; anything else fails with capability_denied.
  • All changes are committed together at the end of the workflow run unless you call ctx.commit() explicitly.
  • If invoke() raises an exception (or the run times out), the entire workflow job is marked as failed and no changes are committed.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Container plugins — a different language, or stricter isolation than a subprocess gives you.
  • The wire protocol — the frame-by-frame reference serve() implements underneath invoke().
  • SDK reference — the full generated civex_plugin_sdk API.

docs.title: Schemas, collections and records
docs.text:
Three ideas carry everything in civex. People new to it mix up the first and the last, so here they are in plain words before anything else.

Schema Collection Record

These colours are used wherever the docs name the three.

docs.title: A blank form, a binder, a filled-in form
docs.text:
A schema is a blank form. When you design the form you decide the boxes (fields) and what is allowed in each box (rules): "Depth, a number, in metres, not below 0". You design it once.

A record is one filled-in copy of that form. Every time you have another sample, you fill in a new copy. You don't redesign the form.

A collection is the binder the filled-in forms go in. Forms of any kind go in any binder. One per study, site or season, as suits you.

flowchart LR
    T["Schema<br/><i>blank form, designed once</i>"]:::rt -->|is the form for| R["Record<br/><i>one filled-in form</i>"]:::rec
    C["Collection<br/><i>the binder</i>"]:::coll -->|holds| R
    classDef rt fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#1e3a8a,color:#1e3a8a
    classDef coll fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#78350f,color:#78350f
    classDef rec fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#14532d,color:#14532d
How many Looks like Made where Schema A handful per project Sample, Site, Visit New schema… in a collection (its own button, apart from New) takes you to the Schemas page with the collection remembered; or Schemas in the sidebar Collection One per study or season survey-2024 Collections → New collection Record Hundreds or thousands Sample 03, North Ridge Inside a collection: New ▸ Sample

docs.title: Which one do I want?
docs.text:
Ask yourself about the thing you're about to create:

  • Can you say "a ___"? "A sample", "a site", "a visit". That is a schema. You will have a few of them in the whole project.
  • Is it "this ___"? "Sample 3", "the North Ridge site", "the visit on 15 March". That is a record. You will have hundreds.
  • Does it have the same boxes as something you already have? Then you want a new record of that type, not a new type.

If you're making a new schema every time you add data, stop

You want New ▸ Sample inside your collection. A schema is the form, not the data. A project with one schema per measurement has no way to list, filter or export them together; a project with one Sample type and five hundred sample records does.

docs.title: Types that go inside other types
docs.text:
A schema can be designed to sit inside another: a Visit goes inside a Site, a Sample goes inside a Visit. Then every sample record you add is filed under the visit it belongs to, and can show and filter on the visit's and the site's fields without you typing them again.

flowchart LR
    S["Site"]:::rt --> V["Visit"]:::rt --> P["Sample"]:::rt
    s1["North Ridge"]:::rec --> v1["2024-03-15"]:::rec --> p1["Sample 01"]:::rec
    v1 --> p2["Sample 02"]:::rec
    s1 --> v2["2024-04-02"]:::rec --> p3["Sample 01"]:::rec
    classDef rt fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#1e3a8a,color:#1e3a8a
    classDef rec fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#14532d,color:#14532d

The top row is the three schemas. Everything below is records. Where you press New schema… decides the nesting: inside a site it starts a schema that goes inside sites. It can't be moved later.

docs.title: The same example everywhere
docs.text:
The rest of the docs use this one example, a field survey:

Schema Its fields Goes inside Site name, location — Visit visited on, team, notes Site Sample number, depth (m), taken at, photo, reading Visit

Collection: survey-2024. Records look like North Ridge › 2024-03-15 › Sample 03.

Next: Five-minute tour →

docs.title: Your first project
docs.text: A project is a folder with a _civex/ folder inside it. Every civex command works on the project it's run in (or below).

docs.title: Try the demo first
docs.text:
civex demo
cd civex-demo
civex serve --open

Demo project created at ./civex-demo
  Schemas     Deployment, Detection
  Collection  amazon-survey-2024
  Records     2 deployments, 7 detections

It's a throwaway project with sample data, so you can click around before setting up your own.

docs.title: Start your own
docs.text:
mkdir my-study && cd my-study
civex init
civex serve --open          # the app, at http://localhost:8000

civex init makes:

_civex/
  config.toml     settings: database, storage volumes, sync, retention
  civex.db        the database (SQLite)
  objects/        stored files
  workflows/      workflow YAML
  plugins/        your own plugins

Which database? If Docker is running, civex init sets up a PostgreSQL container for the project, and otherwise it uses SQLite. civex init --sqlite always picks SQLite. You can move between them later with civex db move. See PostgreSQL.

To start the app with a double-click, civex shortcut puts a shortcut for this project on your Desktop.

Next: Five-minute tour →

docs.title: Install
docs.text: Two ways in: the desktop app (no terminal needed) or the command line. Both include everything: the web app, workflows, PostgreSQL support and the CLI.

docs.title: Command line (recommended)
docs.text:
civex installs with uv, which brings its own Python (3.12+), so you don't need one.

1. Install uv, once per computer:

macOS / LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

Open a new terminal afterwards. (brew install uv, winget install --id=astral-sh.uv -e and pipx install uv work too.)

2. Install civex:

uv tool install civex
civex --version

civex: command not found? Run uv tool update-shell and open a new terminal.

pipx or pip instead 
pipx install civex
# or, in a virtual environment:
pip install civex

Custom plugins still need uv on your PATH. civex doctor says whether it's found.

docs.title: Desktop app
docs.text:
Download it from the release page. It opens civex in its own window, with a project picker.

WindowsmacOSLinux

Run civex-<version>-windows-setup.exe. It installs for you only (no administrator needed). The installer isn't signed yet: if Windows says Windows protected your PC, choose More info → Run anyway.

Open civex-<version>-macos.dmg and drag civex into Applications (macOS 11+, Intel and Apple silicon). It isn't signed yet: the first time, click Done, then System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway.

The window doesn't open on Linux yet. The download still installs civex, so run ~/.local/share/civex/app/bin/civex serve --open and use it in your browser.

The first start downloads civex and its Python (a minute or two, online), into a folder of its own, separate from any uv install. To use the app's copy from a terminal, use Settings → Updates → Command line (on Windows, the installer's Add the civex command to PATH).

With civex already installed by uv, uv tool install --force "civex[desktop]" then civex desktop opens the same window.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
civex update           # the latest release
civex update --check   # just say whether there is one
civex update --pre     # include release candidates

In the app: Settings → Updates, or the notice in the status bar. Either way:

  • It works out how civex was installed (uv, pipx, pip, the desktop app) and updates that copy.
  • Servers running from that copy are stopped, and started again afterwards with the same command (it asks first; --yes skips that).
  • Projects update their databases the next time they open.

docs.title: Something wrong?
docs.text:
civex doctor          # add --fix to clean up stale plugin environments

It checks for another civex earlier on your PATH, missing packages, uv, and whether custom plugins can start. Run inside a project, it checks the project's data too. Each problem comes with the fix.

Next: Your first project →

docs.title: Five-minute tour
docs.text:
One example from start to finish: a Sample schema, a collection to hold samples, a sample record, and a workflow that fills a field by itself. Use the app or the CLI; both build the same project.

If you haven't yet, read Schemas, collections and records first: a schema is the blank form, a record is one filled-in copy.

docs.title: 1. A schema: what a sample looks like
docs.text:
You do this once. Every sample you add afterwards uses this form.

Web UICLI

civex serve --open, then Collections → New collection, named survey-2024. Its page says what to do first: New schema…, which takes you to the Schemas page with the collection remembered. New schema, labelled Sample, opens its page: Add field four times, number (whole number, required), depth (number, unit m), condition (text, allowed values good, damaged, lost) and summary (text). Then back to survey-2024.

civex schema create sample --label "Sample" --description "One physical sample"
civex schema add-field sample number --type integer --required
civex schema add-field sample depth --type float --unit m
civex schema add-field sample condition --type string --choices "good,damaged,lost"
civex schema add-field sample summary --type string

Created schema 'sample'.
Added 'number' (integer (required)) to schema 'sample'.
Added 'depth' (float) {'unit': 'm'} to schema 'sample'.
Added 'condition' (string) {'choices': ['good', 'damaged', 'lost']} to schema 'sample'.
Added 'summary' (string) to schema 'sample'.

docs.title: 2. A collection to hold samples
docs.text:
A collection is the binder: it holds records of any schema.

Web UICLI

Already done: the collection was made first, in step 1.

civex collection create survey-2024 --description "2024 field season"

docs.title: 3. A record
docs.text:
This is the step you repeat: one record per sample, on the same form.

Web UICLI

Open survey-2024, then New ▸ Sample. Fill in number, depth and condition, leave summary blank, and save. Add and add another keeps the form open for the next one.

civex record add --to survey-2024 --schema sample

It asks for each field. Leave summary blank, because the workflow below fills it in:

  number (integer) [required]: 1
  depth (float) []: 12.5
  condition (string) []: good
  summary (string) []:
Added record f623c8d7-eb75-41e1-b2ec-d6feb7f02f7a.

Not a new schema

The second sample is New ▸ Sample again. New schema… is only for a kind of record the collection doesn't have yet.

docs.title: 4. A workflow: fill a field automatically
docs.text:
Create _civex/workflows/sample-summary.yaml (or paste it into Workflows → New workflow):

name: sample-summary
description: Copy the condition into the summary field on new samples.

triggers:
  record_created:
    schema: sample

steps:
  - id: write_summary
    plugin: civex.set_fields@1
    config:
      fields:
        summary: {from_field: condition}    # copy another field of this record

Add another sample (step 3 again) and the workflow runs straight away:

Added record 9a1c47e2-5b3d-4f08-8e61-0c2d7b5a3f90.
  → workflow 'sample-summary' (trigger: record_created)
    ✓ done

civex record find --in survey-2024 --schema sample

ID         number  depth  condition  summary  Created
f623c8d7…  1       12.5   good                2026-10-09
9a1c47e2…  2       8.0    damaged    damaged  2026-10-09

In the app, the second sample's summary shows damaged, and Runs lists the run.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text: To… Read Bring in a folder of files Import files Put samples inside visits and sites Schemas & fields Keep files on an external drive Put files on another drive Work on several computers Sync a project Automate more Fill fields from file names

docs.title: Automation
docs.text: Every time a workflow runs, by a trigger or by hand, it is a run (a job in the CLI). Runs queue and go one at a time: pending → running → completed | failed | cancelled.

docs.title: Runs happen by themselves
docs.text:
Record changes made in the app, over the API or with civex record add/update start their runs straight away. Two cases need a nudge:

civex automation run              # run whatever is waiting, then exit
civex automation run --watch      # keep running new ones (every 5 s; --interval)
civex automation enqueue --workflow my-workflow --record 2d69dc46   # queue without running

The Runs page's Run automation button does the same as civex automation run.

docs.title: Seeing runs
docs.text:
civex automation jobs --status failed     # pending|running|completed|failed|cancelled
civex automation logs <job id>            # one run's log, and what started it
civex automation stats                    # failures per plugin

ID         Workflow      Schema     Record             Trigger  Changed  Status
1adcfb22…  read-sample-…  sample  Sample 01 bfcdc007…  manual   —        failed

The Runs page lists runs with their workflow, record, trigger, result and time. + Filter builds conditions on workflow, status, trigger, schema, time, failure type, error message, failing step and chain depth, like a record filter. It's all in the address, so a filtered list can be linked.

A run's page has three tabs: Summary (what started it, what it did, how it ended), Steps (each step's input and output) and Records touched. Opened from a record's Runs tab, its breadcrumb leads back to that record.

  • What started it: for an edit, exactly which fields changed, from what to what, and which of them the workflow watches. For a run started by another run, which one, and how deep the chain is.
  • Completed with N problems: a run that finished but skipped rows, or left files that matched no record (or matched ambiguously), is never shown as a plain success. The Summary opens with what went wrong.

The status bar at the bottom of every page shows runs in progress (and how many are waiting), a progress bar for a batch, and a notice if a batch ended with failures.

docs.title: Failures: triage and re-run
docs.text:
When runs fail, why they failed on the Runs page groups them by workflow and error, so a thousand failures read as the few causes they are. Show lists a group, and Re-run N repeats it once the cause is fixed.

Tick runs and Re-run N to repeat them (same workflow, record and input), or Re-run all N for everything the filter matches (up to 1,000). Runs that can't be repeated, for example because their record was deleted, are listed with the reason.

Over HTTP: GET /api/jobs?filter=…, GET /api/jobs/failure-groups, POST /api/jobs/rerun (ids or filter), POST /api/workflows/{name}/run-many.

docs.title: Stopping automation
docs.text:
Workflows can trigger each other, or themselves. civex ends a chain after 10 hops, but you can stop everything sooner:

civex automation stop            # pause, and cancel waiting and running runs
civex automation status          # paused or running, and how many wait
civex automation resume
civex automation cancel <job>    # one run
civex automation delete <job>…   # remove runs (a waiting one never starts)
civex automation delete --pending
  • Stop pauses automation: edits start no runs, waiting runs aren't picked up, and manual runs are refused, until Resume. The pause is saved in config.toml ([automation] paused = true), so it holds across restarts and for every terminal.
  • A running run stops before its next step. A step already running finishes first, because a plugin can't be interrupted.
  • Cancelling or deleting a run keeps whatever it already changed in records, which is in their history.

In the app: Stop automation on the Runs page and in the status bar, and a run's × or Cancel run.

docs.title: Collections & records
docs.text: A collection is the binder: it holds records of any schema, one collection per study or season, as suits you, and says who may link to them. A record is one filled-in form of a schema: this site, this sample. If the two blur together, read Schemas, collections and records.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
civex collection create survey-2024 --description "2024 field season" \
  --timezone Europe/London
civex collection show survey-2024

survey-2024
  Records  0
  2024 field season
  Timezone  Europe/London
  Scope     local
Setting Means Scope (--scope) local (default): only records here can link to these. global: any collection can, for shared lists such as species, instruments or people Timezone (--timezone) How times without a UTC offset are read and shown. See Times and timezones 
civex collection create taxonomy --scope global
civex collection list

A reference field links to records in its own collection or in a global one, never in another local collection. A global collection that others link to can't be made local or deleted.

Every collection holds records of every schema, including one made after the collection: there is no list of schemas on a collection to keep up to date.

In the app: Collections → New collection, and Edit on a collection's page.

docs.title: Adding records
docs.text:
Web UICLI

In a collection, the New menu lists the schemas you can add here (New ▸ New site). Inside a record, it lists the types that go inside it (inside a visit: New ▸ New sample). This is the step you repeat; the schema is made once. Add and add another saves and gives you a blank form. A folder of files comes in through a workflow: see Import files.

civex record add --to survey-2024 --schema sample

  Parent record ID (visit): 2d69dc46
  number (integer) []: 3
  depth (float) []: 12.5
  taken_at (datetime) []:
  photo (file) []: /data/IMG_0412.jpg
  reading (file) []:
Added record f623c8d7-eb75-41e1-b2ec-d6feb7f02f7a.

For a type that goes inside another it asks for the parent record first. A file field takes a path, and a reference takes a record id or any unique prefix of one.

docs.title: Finding records
docs.text:
civex record find --in survey-2024 --schema sample --where "number=3" --limit 20
civex record show f623

Record f623c8d7-eb75-41e1-b2ec-d6feb7f02f7a
  Schema    sample
  Parent    2d69dc46 (visit)
  Created   2026-10-09 11:11 UTC
Field     Value
number    3
depth     12.5
photo     IMG_0412.jpg
name      North Ridge  (↑ site)

--where repeats, and all conditions must match. Every record has a UUID, and any unique prefix of it works wherever an id is asked for.

docs.title: The explorer
docs.text:
A collection's page is its records, in one explorer. A record's page says what kind of thing it is above its name, shows its fields (the first few, with Show all, when it has records inside it) and then what it Contains: a chip for each kind inside with its count, a search, and the rows, each a link to that record. It is the same explorer with some of it folded: Filter beside the search opens the filters, saved filters, columns and export, and Charts opens the charts. Rows are ticked there as anywhere, to edit, run a workflow on, move or delete. Files, Exports, Activity and the collection's details are in the ⋯ menu at the top of the page.

The explorer has three ideas. Records are the rows: each row is one record. Filters say which rows you see. Charts count the rows you see.

  • Levels: the collection's schemas top-down (Site → Visit → Sample), with counts. A row shows its children ("3 visits →"). Click to go down, and use the trail to go back up.
  • All kinds, the first of the levels, lists every kind of record at once (in the collection, in every collection on All records, or inside the record you are in), with its name, kind, collection and when it was last edited. It can be searched, filtered by open notes, sorted by those columns, moved and deleted; filtering by a field, charts, Edit… and Run workflow need one kind, so pick one first.
  • Search is scoped to where you are. It looks, ignoring case, in what the records hold: text, numbers, the items of a list (tags, choices) and the names of files. It never matches a file's hash, a reference or a location, so a short search like a3 finds only records that show a3. Typing the start of a record's id (four characters or more) finds that record too. A link or script can narrow it to one field (qin in the address, search_field on the API).
  • + Filter builds AND/OR conditions on this level's fields, a parent's, or any child's: "Visits that have a Sample whose depth is empty" is one condition. Reference values are picked by name.
  • Saved filters keep a filter to come back to: see Saved filters. Save this filter saves yours, and everyone sees it.
  • Columns, beside the count of records, include parents' fields and fields through a reference. Your choice for a kind is remembered in this browser. Click a header to sort.
  • Export takes exactly the rows listed or ticked. See Get files out. It also offers the charts on screen, one or all of them, as tables of their numbers.
  • The files of what's listed (to move between drives, download or free up) are under Files in the page's ⋯ menu. See Files.
  • Charts sit beside the records and count exactly what is listed: see Charts.
  • Under the table, a last row gives, for every record listed (not just the page), the average, smallest and largest of each number column and how many different values each choice column holds.
  • A count such as 3 problems beside the number of records appears only when something needs a look: see Checking the data.
  • Tick rows (shift-click for a range) to Delete or Run workflow on N. Ticking a whole page offers Select all N matching.

Everything is in the address, so a filtered list can be bookmarked and Back undoes a step. Scripts get the same from GET /api/records with schema, within, filter, sort, search and search_field (repeatable: the fields to search in), and from civex record find --in <collection> --schema <kind> --search <text> [--search-field <field>].

A record's Referenced by section counts the records linking to it, per collection, schema and field (GET /api/records/{id}/referrers).

docs.title: Charts
docs.text:
Charts are a panel beside the records. Like the navigation on the left, it folds away with the button at its top and opens again from the Charts button it leaves; another button shows the charts at full width, with Back to records. Drag the line between the records and the charts to make the panel wider (the cards then sit in two columns). These choices are remembered in this browser. Every chart counts exactly the records listed: the same kind, place, search and filters. There are no charts until someone adds one.

  • Click a bar (or a point, or a slice) to filter by its value. The table and the other charts follow, a chip appears above, and clicking it again takes it out. Clear filters beside the chips removes them all. Several bars of one chart are "is any of". The chart you clicked keeps all its bars, with the chosen ones lit, so you can pick another.
  • A filter made from bars is the ordinary filter: it can be changed with + Filter, saved with Save this filter, and shared as a link. When a filter uses a chart's field in a way bars can't show (inside an "or" with another field, or "is not"), the chart counts the filtered records with nothing lit.
  • Which charts. A kind of record says which charts its lists open with (also on its Charts tab on the schema page). A kind starts with none.
  • Add chart opens the builder at full width: the choices on the left and the chart they make on the right, drawn live. First What: what to Show (how many records, or the average, total, smallest or largest of a number, how many have a field filled in, or how many records of a kind beneath are inside them) For each value of a field (a date by year, month, week or day; a number in steps you choose; a location places the records). Then How it is drawn, from the ways that fit: Bars, Line (over dates or steps), Pie (of counts and totals), Table, or Map (for a location). Quick picks fill the choices in for the kind's fields of choices and its first date. Give it a title of your own if you like, then Add chart.
  • Drag a chart by its title to move it. Its ⋮ menu has Edit… (the builder again, on that chart, where you can also give it a title of your own), Larger / Smaller, See numbers (the chart above the records with its table of numbers and Download numbers: CSV, Excel, TSV, JSON; it is in the address, so it is a link and Back closes it), Move up / Move down and Remove. Every change is saved for the kind at once, for everyone, like a saved filter (it takes the right to write records).
  • Add to Analytics page, in a chart's menu, puts it on the Analytics page with the records it counts now.
  • A very large list (over 200,000 records) waits for Show charts.

How values are grouped: a date is kept at the precision it was written, so by month a sample dated only 2019 is its own bar, 2019, month not known. A date and time is grouped in its field's time zone, else the collection's, else UTC. A list (tags, links) puts a record in a bar for each item. There is no median.

A map chart shows the listed records by a location field of their kind or of a kind above it (each record is drawn where that record is). Points that crowd together are one circle with a number; click a record for its name and a link to its page. Opened large it is the full map, and with several location fields one can be picked. It shows the first 10,000 and says so. The base map is the location editor's: coastlines that work offline, plus street detail when a tile address is set in Settings → Map. Narrowing the records by drawing an area is not possible yet.

Scripts get the same numbers from POST /api/records/summary (the list's selectors plus group_by and measures, e.g. site, taken:month, depth:5; count, mean:depth, inside:reading; ?format=csv for a file) and from civex record summarise --in <collection> -s <kind> --by <field>[:month|:5] -m count -m mean:<field> [--csv]; a map's points from POST /api/records/points. Which of these each field type allows is in GET /api/schemas/field-types.

docs.title: Checking the data
docs.text:
Beside the number of records, a count such as 3 problems appears when something in exactly the records listed (the same level, filters and search) needs a look. Nothing is shown when all is well. Click it for the list, counted per field; Back to records returns. For a list of more than 5,000 records the count is not worked out by itself, since that reads every record: open ?show=checks or use the command below.

  • Breaks a rule: a value its field's rules refuse now. Rules are checked when a value is saved, so tightening one later (a lower maximum, fewer choices, a finer date precision) leaves the values already stored as they were. Such a record can still be edited (a save checks only the values it changes), and its broken values can be put right one at a time, by hand or with a bulk edit.
  • Required but empty: a field marked required with no value.
  • Shares a unique key: records in one place with the same values for fields that should be unique together.
  • Broken link: a link to a record that was deleted, or that the record can no longer reach.
  • Missing file: a file that is on no drive here and not on the server.

Each line gives the count and a few of the records. Click it to list them all: open one, or tick them and choose Edit… to put them right in one go (see Changing many records at once). A required field left empty has Show in the list, which adds the condition to the explorer's filter. Unusual numbers are not looked for.

From the command line, with the same options as record find:

civex record check --in survey -s sample                       # one line per field and issue
civex record check --in survey --issue breaks_rule --field depth   # the records, with their ids

Scripts use POST /api/records/quality (the list's selectors) and POST /api/records/quality/records (issue, field, kind, limit, offset).

docs.title: Changing records
docs.text:
civex record update f623        # asks for each field, current value as default

In the app, edit on the record's page. With a file attached, text, number and date fields have from filename to fill them from the file's name.

docs.title: Changing many records at once
docs.text:
To set a field to the same value on many records (mark a batch as checked, fill in the site for a day's uploads), tick them in the explorer, or tick a whole page and choose Select all N matching, then choose Edit…. Pick the field (and Another field for more), enter the value with the field's usual input, or choose Clear to empty it. Before you confirm, the dialog says how many records would change, how many already have the value, which can't take it and why, and how many workflow runs the change would start. From the command line:

civex record set status=checked --id f623 --id a91c            # these records
civex record set status=checked --in survey -s sample -w status=new   # all a list shows
civex record set notes= --in survey -s sample --dry-run         # clear; say what would happen

Each value is read as its field's type. A record takes every change or none: one that can't (a value outside the field's limits, a uniqueness key another record already uses, a field its kind doesn't have) is left as it is and named, and the others are changed. Only a kind's own fields are offered: a field it inherits holds its value on the record above, so edit that kind instead. Files are added one record at a time. Each record's history shows the change, and the whole edit is one event in Activity, where Undo puts it all back (see Undo a mistake).

A big edit runs in the background: the bar at the bottom of the page shows how many records it has changed of how many, and you can go on working (other saves are let in while it runs). Stop ends it where it is: the records changed so far stay changed, and making the same edit again finishes it (or Undo in Activity puts back what was changed).

docs.title: Moving records to another collection
docs.text:
A record can be moved to another collection, or inside another record there. It keeps its id, its values and its history, and takes everything beneath it along; its files stay where they are stored. In the app, tick the records in the explorer and choose Move to…; the dialog says how many records would go, with everything inside them, and whether anything is in the way, before you confirm. From the command line:

civex record move f623 a91c --to archive              # to the top of `archive`
civex record move f623 --to archive --under 7b2e      # inside a record there
civex record move f623 --to archive --dry-run         # say what would happen
civex record move-all survey --schema visit --to archive       # every visit in `survey`

A move is refused whole, and the dialog or the command says why, when a record elsewhere references one being moved (a record may only reference its own collection's records or a global collection's), a uniqueness key is already taken where the records would land, or the kind of record can't sit where it would go. The move is one event in Activity, and a record's history reads it as a change of collection.

docs.title: Notes on records
docs.text:
A note is a short text about a record, "value looks off, re-check the calibration". The record's Notes tab lists its notes as threads: each note with the replies to it underneath, oldest first, with who wrote them and when. Anyone who may change records in the collection can add a note, Reply in a thread, Resolve a thread once it is dealt with (or Reopen it), and delete a note or a reply; only its author can change its words. Replying to a resolved thread opens it again. Deleting the note that starts a thread hides its replies too, and restoring it brings them back.

The record's header says how many threads are still open, and links to its Notes tab. Beside the number of records, any list says N open notes when some of the records listed have one; click it to list them. All open notes on a record's Notes tab lists every record with an open thread, of every kind, in every collection: it is the All records tab of Collections with All kinds picked, filtered with Has open notes, so search and the Open notes filter work on it, and a record opens on its Notes tab. Pick a kind to filter by its fields too. Open notes inside on a record's Notes tab lists the same for everything inside that record. The Open notes column (Columns › Open notes) shows how many threads are open and the first line of the latest, in any list.

civex record note add f623 "depth looks off, re-check the calibration"
civex record note reply 3c1d "it was the sensor, swapped on the 3rd"
civex record note list f623 --open
civex record note resolve 3c1d

Notes are in history and sync to the other computers following the project; two people replying at once are just two replies. Deleting a record hides its notes until it is restored; deleting it permanently removes them, history and all. Scripts use /api/records/{id}/notes and /api/notes/{id}/replies.

docs.title: Signing off records
docs.text: To mark records as checked, or to track a QC state ("pending", "passed", "failed"), add a field for it: a Choice field such as qc with those choices, or a Yes / no field checked. Set it on many records at once with Edit… on the explorer's selection bar (bulk edit), and find what is waiting with the explorer's filter (qc is pending). Being a field, it is in each record's history, syncs, exports, and can start a workflow.

docs.title: Deleting and undoing
docs.text:
civex record delete f623        # with its children, to Recently Deleted
civex record restore f623
civex record delete-all survey-2024 --schema sample

A record linked from another record's reference field can't be deleted without --force, which clears those links.

Every change is in history: a record's History tab, a collection's Activity tab, and Activity in the sidebar for the whole project. Each line says who, what and when, and a bulk operation is one line. Any entry on a record can be reverted:

civex history record f623
civex history revert <entry id>

See Undo a mistake and Deleting & restoring data.

docs.title: Copying a project's data
docs.text: civex bundle export writes schemas, collections, records (their ids kept), the files they cite and the project's workflows to one file, and civex bundle import reads it into another project; in the app, Copy to another project… and Bring in from another project… on the Collections page. It leaves out history and settings. See Back up a project.

docs.title: Deleting & restoring data
docs.text:
Deleting a schema, field, collection or record is reversible. It is hidden from lists, search and exports, and stays restorable until it is purged, which only happens when you choose to. For the short version, see Undo a mistake.

(This is not civex bundle export / civex bundle import, which copy a whole project. See Back up a project.)

docs.title: What a delete takes with it
docs.text:
Delete Also deletes Notes Record Every record inside it, recursively Refused while another record links to it through a reference field, unless --force (which clears those links) Collection Every record in it Schema Every record of that schema, in every collection Records of other schemas beneath them stay Field Nothing Records keep their values for it, shown under Deleted fields on the record 
civex record delete <id>
civex collection delete survey-2024
civex schema delete sample
civex schema remove-field sample depth

docs.title: Restoring
docs.text:
civex trash list                              # newest first; --kind, --search
civex record restore <id>
civex collection restore survey-2024
civex schema restore sample
civex schema restore-field sample <field id>   # id from: civex trash list --kind field

In the app: Activity → Deleted → Restore on the row, or Restore all N for everything listed. Each shows what comes back before doing it, and links to it afterwards.

docs.title: Only what that delete took
docs.text: A delete stamps everything it takes with one time, and a restore brings back exactly that: restoring a collection doesn't bring back a record you had deleted from it the week before.

docs.title: Choosing part of it
docs.text:
A bulk or tree delete is one line in Activity ("Deleted 71 records").

  • Restore on the line brings it all back, parents first.
  • Open the line, tick some records, and Restore N selected. A ticked record whose parent is deleted brings the parent back too, by itself.

For one record:

civex record restore <id>                        # with what was deleted with it
civex record restore <id> --only-this            # leave its children deleted
civex record restore <id> --with-parents         # and the deleted records above it

docs.title: When a restore is refused
docs.text:
Because Do Its collection, schema or parent record is still deleted Restore that first. The app offers Restore the collection "…" instead Another record now has its unique values Change or delete that record. Bulk restores leave these and report them A field: another field took its name Rename or delete that field A field: its schema is deleted Restore the schema first

Records under a deleted record. Rarely, history leaves a live record under a deleted parent. Its page says so, with Restore … to put the parent back, and civex record orphans lists any. civex doctor counts them.

docs.title: Purging (permanent)
docs.text:
civex record purge <id>              # must be deleted first
civex collection purge survey-2024
civex schema purge sample
civex trash purge-expired            # everything deleted longer ago than purge_after_days

In the app: open the deleted item in Activity → Delete permanently.

Purging can't be undone. It removes the thing, everything deleted with it, and every history entry about the records removed. History keeps one note per record (its id, schema, collection, and when it was created and purged), shown in Activity as Gone for good. Deleted fields aren't purged yet. They stay restorable until their schema is purged.

Records purged by an older civex may still have values in history: Settings → Retention offers to remove them (civex retention forget-purged).

docs.title: Retention: keeping less
docs.text:
Deleted items, history and finished workflow runs are kept forever unless you set limits. Nothing is removed by itself: a clean-up applies the limits when you (or a cron job) run it, and always counts first.

Kind Setting ([retention] in config.toml) A clean-up… Deleted items purge_after_days (30), auto_purge_deleted (off) purges items deleted longer ago, only if auto_purge_deleted is on History audit_days (forever) removes older entries Workflow runs run_days (forever) removes finished runs and their logs 
civex retention show                                   # settings, and what would go now
civex retention run --settings                         # apply them (asks first)
civex retention run --history-before 2026-01-01 --dry-run
civex retention run --deleted-before 2026-01-01 --runs-before 2026-01-01

In the app: Settings → Retention, then Clean up now…, or pick dates under Delete everything before a date. You type delete to confirm.
