Always kept: history about anything you can still restore, each existing thing's first and latest entry, runs still waiting or running, and a deleted parent while anything beneath it remains. Files freed by a clean-up are removed by storage clean-up (civex store gc).

docs.title: Exports
docs.text: An export turns a selection of records into a folder (or zip) of their files, named and arranged by the records, with tables of the records beside them if you want. For a walkthrough, see Get files out as folders, zips or tables.

docs.title: Paths
docs.text:
A file's path is the names of the records above it, then the record that holds it, then the file's name:

North Ridge/2024-03-15/Sample 03/photo.jpg
  • Names are the record names shown in the app (the schema's name template).
  • The record holding a file is a folder too, so many samples each holding photo.jpg never clash.
  • Two records with the same name in one place get a short id each (2024-03-15~3f9c01ab). Nothing else changes.
  • Paths start below where you export from: exporting within North Ridge drops North Ridge/. Across several collections, the collection's name leads.

docs.title: Layouts
docs.text:
Layout Gives Use when tree (default) North Ridge/2024-03-15/Sample 03/photo.jpg You want the hierarchy grouped North Ridge/2024-03-15/Samples/photo.jpg Files of one kind together, under their parents flat photo.jpg One folder for everything

Where records share a folder (grouped, flat), two different files with the same name are told apart by their record (Sample 02 - photo.jpg).

docs.title: How the folder is made
docs.text:
Method How Space Where Link (--mode link, default) Read-only hard links to the stored files; copies of any it can't link None, except the copies _exports/<name> on the drive holding most of the files (_civex/exports/<name> for the default volume) Copy (--mode copy --to <drive>) Real copies The files' size, checked first On the drive you pick Zip (civex files download x.zip) One file The files' size Where you say

Linked files are ordinary files to Windows, WSL and every program, but they are the stored files, so civex makes them read-only: a program can open them but not save over them. Links can't cross drives, and exFAT and FAT32 drives can't link at all, so a file that can't be linked is copied into the folder instead (the room for those copies is checked first). How the files are spread over drives never stops a folder being made; to avoid the copies, gather the files onto one drive first (civex files gather … --to <drive>). Symlinks are never used, because they break when a drive is unplugged.

An export folder holds a .civex-export.json listing what civex put there. Running the export again updates only the difference, and removing it (civex files exports remove) deletes exactly those files and nothing you added.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Formats: csv, tsv, xlsx (numbers stay numbers), json (joined values nest), jsonl (one record per line, for very large tables). A point is written lat, lon and a list as JSON in every format.

A table has three independent choices:

Choice Options Rows One kind of record, e.g. every Visit Where it's written Once at the top, or in each folder of a kind ("a table of each Visit's Samples") Columns Own fields, fields of the records above, one hop through a reference (species.common), id, schema, parent_record_id (the record it is inside), created_at, updated_at

A column holding files gives each file's path in the export, so the table and the folder agree. A details sheet is a table in a record's own folder with one field per line. Tables in folders need the tree layout.

From the CLI, --table csv makes one table per kind at the top. On a saved export, --table-of and --table-in set a single table's rows and folder:

# in each visit's folder, a table of its samples
civex schema exports add site "Per visit" --kind sample \
  --table csv --table-of sample --table-in visit

For several tables, describe them in JSON:

civex schema exports add site "Sheets" --kind sample --tables-json '[
  {"format": "csv", "kind": "sample", "where": "visit"},
  {"format": "csv", "kind": "sample", "where": "sample", "shape": "fields"}
]'

docs.title: Saved exports
docs.text:
A saved export belongs to a schema and starts from it: it takes that kind and everything inside it. Saved on Site, it is offered on every Site, Visit and Sample page, and on collections. It never names a collection or a record; those are where it is run. It also says how it is handed over, so running it asks nothing: --method link (a folder of links on the files' drive, the default), copy with --to <drive> (real copies), or zip (one file). An export can be saved before there is anything to export; it takes whatever records and files come later.

civex schema exports add site "Photo files" --kind sample --field photo --layout flat
civex schema exports add site "For the lab" --method copy --to archive
civex schema exports list site --available   # every export that runs within a site
civex schema exports set site "Photo files" --layout grouped --method zip
civex schema exports remove site "Photo files"

civex files export --export "site/Photo files" --in survey-2024 --name photos
civex files list   --export "site/Photo files" --under <site id>

schema exports add --filter takes a JSON filter tree. To export what a saved view lists, use civex files export --view schema/view.

docs.title: In the app
docs.text:
• Export menus are on any list of records (it takes the rows listed, or the rows ticked), on a record's page (every file beneath it), and on a collection's Exports tab.
  • The Exports page in the sidebar is where exports are defined: Saved lists them (narrow with Starts from…, run with Run on…), Made lists folders on disk and removes them.
  • The builder has three steps:
    1. What to include: one card per kind, top down. Tick the files to include and the tables to write (One spreadsheet of all Visits, Each Visit's details, as a sheet in its folder, A list of each Visit's Samples, in its folder). A ticked table shows its format; Customise… opens its name and columns. Only some Samples… adds a filter.
    2. Layout: how the folders nest.
    3. Save: a name, how it is handed over (folder of links, copies on a drive, or a zip), and a preview of what it makes with the data you have now. With no data yet the preview says so and the export still saves.
  • A saved export in an Export menu runs straight away, the way it was saved. Export… in the same menu is a one-time export, which asks how to hand it over at the end.

docs.title: Files
docs.text: A file field holds one file and a file_list field holds several. civex stores the bytes once per drive, named by their content hash, and the record keeps a reference: {sha256, filename, size}. Where the bytes live is covered in Storage volumes. Getting files back out as folders is in Exports.

docs.title: Attaching files
docs.text:
Web UICLIAPI

On a record's page, drop files on the field (or choose them). Each one uploads with progress and is attached at once; there's nothing to save. A file the field won't take (wrong type, too big) is refused before uploading. You're only asked to confirm when a file would go: removing one, or replacing a single-file field's file.

Attaching saves the record, so workflows watching the field run straight away.

civex record add and civex record update ask for a path:

  reading (file) []: /data/readings/20240315_090000.csv
  photos (file_list): /data/photo1.jpg
  photos (file_list): /data/photo2.jpg
  photos (file_list):                      ← blank to finish

Upload, then put the returned reference in the field:

curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/api/files?collection=survey-2024" -F "file=@photo.jpg"
# → {"sha256": "3f9c…", "filename": "photo.jpg", "size": 200000}

?collection= sends the file to that collection's home drive.

A removed or replaced file stays stored until clean-up removes it.

docs.title: Restricting what a field accepts
docs.text:
civex schema add-field sample photo --type file --accept ".jpg,.png"
civex schema add-field document pdf --type file --accept ".pdf" --max-size 10485760   # 10 MB

--accept uses the HTML accept format (extensions or MIME types, case-insensitive). The app checks both before uploading. The API checks them when the record is saved, not on upload: POST /api/files stores any file, and a record citing one the field doesn't accept is refused.

Download names. A file field can rename its file on download with a template, such as {species.common}_{site}_{take:02}, using fields of the record and the records above it. The stored file and its original name are unchanged. See Naming records and files.

docs.title: Where a file is
docs.text:
With one drive and nothing wrong, the app shows nothing extra. Otherwise:

  • A file on a drive that can't be reached is always marked with the drive's name. Its chip says what to do, such as which drive to plug in.
  • With several drives, each file shows a chip naming its drive. Click it for where it is, whether it opens, and More details (every copy, its path on disk, its hash, what else uses it).
  • A record whose files are split or unavailable gets a one-line summary: 3 files stored on archive (2), default (1) · Split across 2 volumes.
civex store where bfcdc007              # a record's files and their drives
civex store where bfcdc007 --details    # + paths on disk, what else uses each

Over HTTP, every file value in a record response carries location, and GET /api/files/{sha256}/info has the details. GET /api/files/{sha256} downloads the file (?filename= names it). It answers 503, naming the drive, when the file is on one that isn't connected.

docs.title: Working on many files
docs.text:
Files, in the ⋯ menu at the top of a collection's or a record's page, lists the files of exactly the records listed and everything beneath them, under the same filters. Filter Visits to site = North Ridge, open Files, and you see their photos and readings. Back to records returns to the list.

  • Each row is a file as stored. A file three records use is one row, and Used by N records lists them.
  • A bar shows where they all are: each drive, an unplugged drive, not on this computer (for a synced project), and missing. Click a place to list only its files.
  • Kinds of file narrows to some file fields.
  • The list is in the order the records were added, as the records list is. Sort it by size or by where the files are.
  • The search box finds a file by the name it was added under, or by its record or a record above it, as searching the records does.

Tick files, then:

Action Does Change storage drive… Moves them onto one drive. Only the listed records' references move: a copy other records point at stays where it is Download to this computer Fetches files only on the sync server Free up space… Removes this computer's copies of files the server holds

The same in a terminal, using the selection options of civex files, plus --on for a place and --name for a file or record name:

civex files list   --in survey-2024 --on field-ssd
civex files gather --in survey-2024 --on field-ssd --to archive
civex files fetch  --under 2d69dc46
civex files free   --in survey-2024 --name ".jpg"

docs.title: On a project that syncs
docs.text: A file another device added downloads when you open or export it, and in the background for collections this computer keeps. See Which files a computer keeps.

docs.title: Backing up
docs.text: A bundle (civex bundle export) carries the files the records cite unless --no-files; for a full backup copy _civex/objects/ and every volume folder. See Back up a project.

docs.title: Hosting civex
docs.text: A host that serves many projects (civex-hub) serves the same built frontend at a path of its own and hands it a boot object. render_app_page(dist, base=..., boot=...) (civex.server.app_page) writes the base path into <base href> and the boot object into window.__CIVEX__, before the app starts.

docs.title: The boot object
docs.text:
Field Meaning login_url Where to send a person whose session ended (a 401); ?next= carries where to return. extensions ES modules to load. Each registers components into named slots. chrome "embedded": the host draws the chrome. civex hides its top bar, footer, left navigation rail and the Settings item, and draws only the page. Anything else is civex's own chrome. theme A map of CSS custom properties set on :root before the first paint, for example {"--color-accent": "#0a5"}. Only names starting -- with string values apply. They are inline styles, so they hold in light and dark mode alike: pick tokens that work in both. brand {name, logo_url}: shown in civex's own top bar in place of "civex". Not shown when chrome is "embedded".

With chrome: "embedded" the top bar's controls (Jump to, sync, Ask AI) go with it; Ctrl+K still opens the palette, and the host provides the rest.

Without chrome, theme and brand the app looks as it does on a desktop.

docs.title: A host header: the app.header slot
docs.text:
An extension registers a component in app.header and it is drawn at the top of every page, above civex's own top bar (or alone, when embedded). It is given { path }, the app's current path and query, without the base path.

const { register, shared } = window.__CIVEX__
const { createElement: h } = shared.react
register('app.header', ({ path }) => h('nav', null, `Project tabs at ${path}`), {
  id: 'hub-header',
})

Extensions use the app's React and router through window.__CIVEX__.shared.

docs.title: Following navigation
docs.text: On every route change (and once at start) the app dispatches a civex:navigate CustomEvent on window, whose detail.path is the path and query within the app. A host page script listens for the event directly, or, if it loads later, reads window.__CIVEX__.navigate.current() first. Extensions can use window.__CIVEX__.navigate.on(fn), which calls fn(path) now and on each change, and returns a function that stops listening; navigate.current() returns the path.

docs.title: Features a host should switch off
docs.text:
A host owns identity, access, settings and where data lives, so it narrows project.features (civex.domain.features) and the app hides, and the server refuses, what it turned off. GET /api/status/features returns what is on and every feature that exists, so a host sees the whole list. A route of a feature that is off answers 501; the app shows "Not available here" at its address as well as hiding its navigation item.

The rule for settings_* features. A settings feature hides that section of civex's app and refuses only the routes that edit that section's stored settings. It never refuses an operational route a host's own UI drives (the device invites, approvals and revokes under /remote/authority*, the retention clean-up under /retention/*): those stay governed by the host's own gate and by permissions. Reading a setting is never refused either: the app reads some of them everywhere. /settings/shortcut stays under desktop. settings is the umbrella: with it off, every settings_* section counts as off, in the server and the app (features.enabled), and PATCH /settings/identity is refused too.

For a hub that owns all settings, leave out of features:

Feature What goes settings The whole Settings area and its navigation item, and every section below. Also refuses editing /settings/identity. settings_appearance Appearance; refuses edits to /settings/ui. settings_retention Retention; refuses editing /settings/retention (the clean-up routes stay). settings_map Map tiles; refuses editing /settings/map. settings_advanced Advanced; refuses changing /settings/command-line. settings_devices The Devices section of the app (what a hosted project shows in place of Sync); no route is refused. settings_members Members & access, which the host manages on its own pages. App only.

Also leave out the features that need a machine: volumes, store_admin, db_admin, local_workflows, plugin_editor, terminal, updates, logs, ai, open_folder, desktop, server_path_export, plugin_install and remote_dial.

releases is the one feature a host turns on. It is off by default and not part of a project on a machine: a release (a permanent, citable, frozen copy) is published by a host, never made on a personal device, and never synced. With it on, /releases/* (making, correcting, withdrawing, yanking, listing, reading, comparing, the files, and /releases/{name}/bundle, one bundle with its files that civex clone <repo-url> --release NAME reads into a new project) and the app's Releases pages exist; with it off they answer 404 and the app hides them. Pair it with the release permission below.

The top-bar sync button and /sync/review need no feature: they appear only for a project that follows a remote, never for a hosted authority.

docs.title: Permissions: the host decides, civex enforces
docs.text: civex keeps no roles, members or grants. The host works out what each request's caller may do and hands civex a Permissions in Project.permissions (from your project_resolver); civex enforces exactly that, in the services (so the HTTP API and the CLI agree) and in the sync authority (so a device is held to what its person is). A project in a folder on a machine has Permissions.everything() and is held to nothing.

docs.title: The actions
docs.text:
Action What it lets the caller do read see the project's records, history and files write_records add, change and restore records change_structure change kinds of record, fields and collections; available only to a caller who can read every collection (Permissions drops it when read is limited). Deleting a field also needs delete add_files cite or upload a file a record did not hold delete_files let go of a file a record held delete delete records, collections and kinds of record notes write, change and delete notes on records views save and change filters, exports and the Analytics page manage_members the host's own; civex has no member endpoints to guard manage_devices every /remote/authority* route: invite, approve, revoke devices release make, correct, withdraw and yank a release (with the releases feature on). A host that says nothing about it gives it wherever it gives change_structure, so existing roles behave as before; say it (or lacking it) to separate the two

manage_files still works as a name for add_files plus delete_files: grant it, deny it or ask it, and it means both. It is never reported on its own.

Every action can be limited to collections, read included:

Permissions.of("read", "write_records", "notes",
               collections=[a, b],          # the actions, only in a and b
               read_collections=[a, b, c])  # may see a, b and c; others do not exist
Permissions.of("read", "write_records").without(["write_records"], [x])  # all but x

read stays project-wide unless you pass read_collections (or put a read scope or denial in Permissions yourself). A collection created later is seen exactly when the rule says: always under "all but these", never under a list.

Notes and views used to be part of writing records. A host that says nothing about notes or views (neither grants nor denies them) keeps that: they go where write_records goes, denials included. Say anything about one, or call .lacking("notes", "views"), and it is yours to decide.

docs.title: A collection without read is not there
docs.text:
For a caller who cannot read a collection, civex behaves as if it did not exist:

  • it is absent from lists, counts, search, summaries, charts, dashboards, saved views, exports and downloads, history and audit (a record's entries too), notes, referrers and file lists;
  • asking for it, or for anything in it, directly is a 404, never a 403, so its existence is not given away;
  • writes that would touch it (creating a record in it, moving a record into it, referencing a record of it) are refused the same way, and a record's file downloaded by hash is a 404 unless a record the caller can read holds it too;
  • a dashboard card over it stays in the layout and says "not available to you".

This is one rule at the one layer every query goes through (civex.db.read_scope), not a check each route remembers. What it does not hide, by design:

  • Kinds of record and their fields are project-wide. civex has no per-schema scope: a collection holds records of every kind. A hidden collection's records are hidden; the names of kinds and fields remain visible to everyone who can read anything, so do not put secrets in kind or field names.
  • A reference from a record the caller can read to a record in a hidden global collection shows the raw id, with no label, and cannot be followed (404).
  • Routers and actions about the project as a whole answer 403 to a caller who cannot read every collection: storage, transfers, buckets, retention, releases, the database pages and index builds, the history-storage pages, workflow runs and the job list and its analytics, importing a bundle, and deleting, restoring or purging a kind of record or setting its uniqueness rules (these reach the records of every collection, and skipping the hidden ones would then fail on them and show that they exist). A push that deletes or restores a kind, or sets uniqueness rules, is refused the same way.
  • History lists an entry only when its subject is visible: entries of a release (its bundle and counts cover the whole project) and of any entry type civex does not know are not shown to such a caller; kinds, fields, filters and dashboards are.
  • A collection's name is unique across all collections, hidden and deleted ones included. Creating or renaming onto a name one of them holds is refused with the same 409 as any taken name.
  • Counting records for a caller limited to some collections is exact up to 100,000 and then reports 100,000, flagged as an estimate (estimated: true): the planner's figure covers the hidden collections, and an exact count of a huge project is a scan.
  • A record moved out of a hidden collection carries its earlier history with it.
  • Deleting a record that records in a hidden collection still refer to is refused ("referenced by records you cannot see"), forced or not, so nothing is left dangling and nothing hidden is touched. Deleting a global collection, or making it local, is refused the same way while records the caller cannot see point into it (a push that deletes it too).
  • Content with no use by any record (just uploaded, or left behind until clean-up) is not tied to a collection, so anyone who knows its hash can fetch it.
  • Citing a file you cannot download. A save through the API that cites a file the record did not hold must cite one that is here and that the caller could download. A hash used only by records the caller cannot read, and a hash that is not here at all, are refused in the same words ("That file is not available.", 422), so citing is neither a way to read a file nor a way to learn whether the project holds it. Upload first, then cite. Residual, for pushes: a device sends its changes before its files, so a pushed record may cite a hash not here yet; that is accepted, while a hash only hidden records hold is rejected. Someone who already knows a hash (it is the hash of the content) can therefore tell, from a device, whether the project holds that content; and a hash cited before its bytes arrive becomes readable by the citer once a hidden record's bytes land under it, which gives the BYTES to someone who knew only the hash. Closing it needs the push path to refuse unknown hashes, which devices (files go after their changes) cannot do yet. For a device (once sync serves such callers), a file it may not read is also answered as "missing" and offered an upload target, never "already here".
  • A record's id. Changing or deleting a record held in a collection the device cannot read is answered as the same change to an id that is not here. A create that names an id which exists in such a collection is refused, while a new id is taken: ids are random, so this tells only someone who already has the id.
  • A record is settled in its parent's collection, so a pushed child's placement is judged where it ends up (read and write), and a parent the device cannot see is refused like one that does not exist.

docs.title: Scope strings are normalised
docs.text: A collection scope (collection:<uuid>) may arrive in any spelling of the id (upper case, no hyphens): Permissions rewrites each to the one canonical form when it is built, so a rule never depends on how it was written. A grant that cannot be read grants nothing; a denial that cannot be read denies the action everywhere.

docs.title: Devices and pushes
docs.text:
Project.permissions is used for a device's sync requests too: your resolver sees the device's request and should return the permissions of the person the device belongs to. A push is judged with the same object: a change in a collection the device may not read or write, a file it may not add or let go of, or a record that is held here in such a collection (whatever the push says) is refused through the ordinary rejected-change path with code: "permission".

Project.push_accepted is called once after a push has been committed and took at least one change, with a civex.domain.sync.PushAccepted (device, actor, the ids of the changes taken, counts by status and by kind, and their feed numbers). A change a device sends again (answered as before, nothing done) is not counted. It replaces reading push responses in middleware; an exception in it is logged and never fails the push.

docs.title: Devices that may not read everything (sync)
docs.text:
For a device whose person may not read some collections, the authority (your app's /sync/v1, with the permissions your resolver gave that request) sends only what the person may read: the feed, a joining device's copy, hello.counts and the files used only by hidden collections. A change to a hidden collection is never sent; a record moved across the line is sent as its removal or its full creation. Releases are not synced at all (protocol 6). The device's own pushes are refused through the ordinary not-taken path when they would write into, or point at, what it may not read.

  • Widening is automatic: the next sync's hello lists the readable collections (protocol 5), and the device reads the ones it did not have. Nothing for the host to do. Narrowing stops delivery at once, but data already on a device cannot be clawed back; say so wherever your product promises revocation.
  • A device whose person may not read the whole project must be on sync protocol 5 or later: on an older one it is answered 426 with "update civex on this device" (it could not be told how far the authority looked, nor of a collection it is given). A device whose person reads everything is served on any version, as before.
  • The feed's numbers are shared by everyone, so a device can see gaps (that something happened it may not see), never what.

docs.title: Logging & telemetry
docs.text:
civex writes structured logs locally and can optionally send crash reports to an error-tracking service. The two are separate:

  • Logging — a local record of what happened. On by default. Stays on your machine.
  • Telemetry — crash reports sent off your machine so the maintainer can see errors across installs. Off by default, opt-in only.

docs.title: Logging (default)
docs.text:
When you run civex serve, logs go to two places:

  • Console — human-readable, colored output when attached to a terminal; single-line JSON when piped or captured.
  • File — rotating JSON lines at _civex/logs/civex.log (5 MB × 3 backups), ideal for grepping or shipping to a log tool.

Every HTTP request gets a correlation id (returned in the X-Request-ID response header and attached to every log line for that request). Values that look like credentials (api_key, token, authorization, password, …) are automatically redacted to *** before anything is written. The _civex/logs/ directory is git-ignored.

Set the level from the CLI (overrides config):

civex serve --log-level DEBUG      # DEBUG | INFO | WARNING | ERROR

Or configure it in _civex/config.toml:

[logging]
level = "INFO"          # default INFO
json_console = false    # omit for auto (color on a TTY, JSON otherwise)
to_file = true          # write _civex/logs/civex.log

docs.title: Every log in one place
docs.text:
civex keeps a few logs besides the project's, each where the thing that writes it can put it:

Log What writes it project This project's server (_civex/logs/civex.log) desktop The desktop app's window launcher The desktop app's launcher: installing and updating civex update Updates of a civex serve, run after it closed serve-<port> A server an update stopped and started again (off Windows)

Settings → Logs shows them all: the latest lines, newest first, with a level filter and search, Follow for new lines, Download, and Open folder. Anything in the app that mentions a log links there (a failed update, a sync that can't reach its server). A workflow run's log is on the run's own page.

From a terminal:

civex logs list                         # which there are, and where
civex logs show                         # the project's latest 50 lines
civex logs show launcher -n 200         # another log
civex logs show --level error -f        # errors only, and keep following
civex logs path update                  # where it is
civex logs open                         # its folder in the file manager

The project's log is JSON lines, so other tools read it too:

cat _civex/logs/civex.log | jq 'select(.level == "error")'   # errors only

docs.title: Error responses
docs.text: Expected errors (not found, validation, conflicts) return a clear message and the right HTTP status. Unexpected server errors return a generic 500 {"detail": "Internal server error", "request_id": "..."} — the full traceback is written to the logs only, never leaked to the client. Quote the request_id when reporting a problem to find the matching log line.

docs.title: Telemetry (opt-in crash reporting)
docs.text:
Nothing is sent off your machine unless you turn this on. It uses Sentry and reports only exception stack traces (no request bodies, send_default_pii=False, no performance tracing).

  1. Nothing to install — the Sentry SDK ships with civex.

  2. Provide a DSN — either in _civex/config.toml:

[telemetry]
dsn = "https://<key>@<org>.ingest.sentry.io/<project>"
environment = "local"

or via an environment variable (takes effect without editing config):

export CIVEX_SENTRY_DSN="https://<key>@<org>.ingest.sentry.io/<project>"

With no DSN (the default), telemetry is a no-op even though the SDK is installed.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text: A project uses SQLite unless you choose otherwise. PostgreSQL suits bigger projects and many people working at once: record data is stored as JSONB with indexes. The driver is included with civex.

docs.title: New project
docs.text:
civex init starts a PostgreSQL container for the project when Docker is available, and uses SQLite otherwise:

civex init            # Docker PostgreSQL if possible
civex init --sqlite   # always SQLite

The container is named civex-<project>, with its own port and volume, and its URL is written to _civex/config.toml.

docs.title: Existing project: move it
docs.text:
civex db move copies everything (records, history, runs), checks the copy, and only then switches over:

civex db move --to docker
civex db move --to postgres --host db.example.org --database civex --user ada
civex db move --to sqlite
civex db moves            # past moves
civex db revert <id>      # switch back
  • The original database is never changed, so stopping halfway leaves the project as it was.
  • Row counts of every table and a sample of records are compared before switching.
  • The destination must be empty.
  • revert switches back. Anything added since stays in the new database.

In the app: Settings → Database → Move to another database…. Past moves and Switch back are on its Move history tab.

Files aren't in the database, so a move doesn't touch them.

One database per project

Schema and collection names are unique per database, and civex has no other separation between projects. Two projects pointed at one database will mix. civex db setup-docker gives each project its own container. If you run PostgreSQL yourself, give each project its own database.

docs.title: Your own server
docs.text:
civex db setup-postgres                               # finds a local server, asks the rest
civex db setup-postgres --url postgresql+psycopg2://civex:secret@db:5432/civex_myproject

This points the project at an empty database and builds it. It doesn't copy data: for that, use db move. In the app: Settings → Database → Advanced → connection URL → Test and switch.

civex db setup-docker likewise starts a new empty container, and refuses if the current database has records.

docs.title: Status and upgrades
docs.text:
civex db status     # connection, migration state, Docker container
civex db migrate    # update the database structure now

New civex versions update the database structure the next time a project opens. Settings → Database shows the connection and offers Update it when an update is waiting.

docs.title: Measuring a project from a host
docs.text:
A host that runs many projects against one PostgreSQL server (one schema each, chosen by the engine's search_path) can meter them with civex.usage.project_usage(engine) instead of reading civex's tables:

from civex.usage import project_usage

u = project_usage(engine)
u.stored_bytes, u.stored_objects      # distinct files in the object store
u.records_estimate, u.records_exact   # planner estimate on PostgreSQL

It reads only, so a read replica's engine works. Records come from pg_class.reltuples (no scan; as fresh as the last ANALYZE); a table never analysed is counted up to 100,000 and then reported as "at least that many". Each statement has a 5 second timeout, and a figure that could not be had in time is None.

docs.title: Using civex from Python
docs.text:
A script, a notebook or a pipeline step can open a project directly with civex.open(). Nothing else needs to be running: no server and no app. You get the same services the civex command and the app use, in your own process, so whatever works there works here, with the same checks, history and automations.

import civex

with civex.open("~/fieldwork") as project:
    for page in project.record_svc.iter_find("survey-2024", schema_name="sample"):
        for record in page:
            print(record.id, record.data)

civex.open(path) finds the project at path or in a folder above it (like git does), and opens the one around the current directory when no path is given.

docs.title: Saving changes
docs.text:
Inside a with block, everything the block did is saved when it finishes, and nothing is saved when it raises. A failed pipeline step therefore leaves the project as it was:

with civex.open() as project:
    project.record_svc.add("survey-2024", "sample", {"depth": 1.5, "site": "A3"})
    project.record_svc.add("survey-2024", "sample", {"depth": 2.0, "site": "A4"})
# both saved here, or neither

Without a with block, call project.commit() to save and project.close() when you're done.

docs.title: Reading into pandas
docs.text:
project.frame(collection, schema) gives the records of one kind as a pandas DataFrame whose columns already have their types. It is the same table an export writes (the same columns, the same rule for fields of the records above and for links), with Python values instead of text:

import civex

with civex.open() as project:
    samples = project.frame("survey-2024", "sample")

samples.dtypes
# id                  string
# depth              float64
# count                Int64      (whole numbers; a blank stays <NA>)
# taken    datetime64[UTC]      (date and time, in UTC)
# day           datetime64      (a date field that takes whole days)
# region            category      (a choice)
# site_name           string      (a field of the site each sample is inside)
# place               object      (the location as GeoJSON)
# place_lat, place_lon float64    (for points)
# audio               string      (where the file is on this computer)

What each kind of field becomes:

Field In the DataFrame Whole number, decimal, true/false Int64, float64, boolean (blanks stay blank) Date a date (datetime64) when the field takes whole days. A field that also takes a year or a month keeps its values as written ("2019", "2019-06"), because a year is not its first day; civex.domain.partial_dates.period(value) gives the first and last day it covers Date and time datetime64 in UTC (samples.taken.dt.tz_convert("Europe/London") for local time) Location the GeoJSON geometry, plus <field>_lat and <field>_lon for points (geo="split", the default); geo="geojson" leaves out the two columns, geo="wkt" gives well-known text (POINT (-3.41 56.12)) for shapely or GeoPandas File the path of the file on this computer, ready for open() (files="path", the default); files="name" gives its name. A file that isn't here right now (a drive not plugged in, files kept in a bucket, only on the server) gives its name List of files, tags, links to several records a list Link to a record the record's name (references="name", the default) or its id (references="id") Choice category Text string

A file's path is where civex keeps it, named by its content, so it has no extension: libraries that read the file's own header (soundfile, Pillow, pandas' readers) open it as it is. Read it, never write to it.

Columns. columns=[...] picks and orders them. A column is a field of the kind, a field of a record it sits inside (a sample inside a site has the site's fields as columns, by their names), a field of the record a link points at (lab.title), or one of id, schema, parent_record_id, created_at, updated_at. Without columns the table is the id and every field, those of the records above included. A name that isn't any of these raises ValidationError.

with civex.open() as project:
    df = project.frame(
        "survey-2024",
        "sample",
        columns=["id", "site_name", "place", "depth", "audio", "lab.title"],
        where={"field": "depth", "op": "gt", "value": 10},
    )

df.attrs["units"]   # {"depth": "m"}: each decimal field's unit
df.attrs["types"]   # {"depth": "float", "place": "geo", ...}: each column's civex type

import soundfile
for path in df.audio.dropna():
    signal, rate = soundfile.read(path)

A decimal field with a unit keeps its name as the column's; every value is in that unit, which df.attrs["units"] names.

Which records. where is a filter, either the explorer's (a dict, as saved in a view) or a list of "field=value" terms; search="..." and search_fields=[...] look for text as the app's search box does; within= takes a record id and keeps only what is beneath it. The collection may be None for every collection.

project.rows(...) takes the same arguments and gives a list of dicts with the same values (a datetime.date, a UTC datetime, a list), for code that doesn't use pandas. Both read the records a page at a time, so the memory used is the table's own. They are project.file_access_svc.frame(query, ...) and typed_rows(query, ...) over a RecordQuery.

For records as civex holds them (field values as stored, names as keys), record_svc.iter_find(collection, schema_name=...) returns them a page at a time. To narrow it, pass filters=["site=A3"] (each entry is field=value) together with schema_name. A field's name only means something within its schema, so a filter without one raises ValidationError. search="..." looks for text, ignoring case, in the records' values (text, numbers, list items and file names; never a file's hash, a reference or a location), or the start of a record's id. search_fields=["site"] looks only in those fields of schema_name. find, count, iter_find, find_by_schema and count_by_schema_search all take them, and match the same way.

docs.title: Summaries
docs.text:
record_svc.summarise(query, request) groups the records a RecordQuery lists and works out measures over each group, in the database (one query, however many records). It is what the explorer's charts and civex record summarise use:

import civex
from civex.domain.query import RecordQuery
from civex.domain.summary import GroupBy, Measure, SummaryRequest

with civex.open() as project:
    result = project.record_svc.summarise(
        RecordQuery(dataset="survey-2024", schema="sample"),
        SummaryRequest(
            group_by=[GroupBy("region", schema="site"), GroupBy("taken", bucket="month")],
            measures=[Measure("count"), Measure("mean", "depth")],
        ),
    )
    for row in result.rows:
        print([g.label for g in row.groups], row.values)
    print("total", result.total)

A GroupBy names a field of the kind summarised, or of a kind above it (schema=); bucket (year, month, week, day) groups a date, bin a number into ranges that wide. A Measure is count (records) or one of filled, distinct, min, max, mean, sum over a field. Each group value carries lower/upper for a range or period, and each row where, the filter tree that lists exactly its records (pass it as filter_tree). parse_group_by and parse_measure read the CLI's written forms (site.region, taken:month, mean:depth).

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
record_svc.points(query, field, schema=None, limit=10_000) gives where the records a RecordQuery lists are: each one with a value in the location field field (of the kind listed, or of schema, a kind above it), with its id, its name and the GeoJSON geometry, oldest first. It is what the explorer's Map draws, and a quick way into a plotting library:

import civex
from civex.domain.query import RecordQuery

with civex.open() as project:
    found = project.record_svc.points(
        RecordQuery(dataset="survey-2024", schema="sample"), "place", schema="site"
    )
    for p in found.points:
        print(p.name, p.geometry["type"], p.geometry["coordinates"])
    if found.truncated:
        print(f"first {len(found.points)} of {found.total}")

docs.title: Checking the data
docs.text:
quality_svc.check(query) says what in the records a RecordQuery lists needs a look, per kind and field (values their field's rules now refuse, required fields left empty, shared unique keys, broken links, missing files), and quality_svc.records_with(query, issue, field=...) lists exactly the records with one issue, ready for record_svc.bulk_edit(..., ids=...):

import civex
from civex.domain.query import RecordQuery

with civex.open() as project:
    query = RecordQuery(dataset="survey-2024", schema="sample")
    for kind in project.quality_svc.check(query).kinds:
        for line in kind.issues:
            print(kind.schema, line.field, line.issue, line.count)
    found, total = project.quality_svc.records_with(
        query, "breaks_rule", field="depth", limit=1000
    )
    project.record_svc.bulk_edit({"depth": None}, ids=[f.record_id for f in found])

quality_svc.check_field(schema, field, restrictions={...}) counts what a rule would leave behind before you change it.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
note_svc adds notes to a record, replies in their threads, resolves and deletes them, lists a record's threads (each with its replies), and counts the open threads among the records a query lists; the @open_notes filter finds the records with one:

with civex.open() as project:
    note = project.note_svc.add("f623", "depth looks off, re-check the calibration")
    project.note_svc.reply(str(note.id), "it was the sensor")
    project.note_svc.resolve(str(note.id))
    open_ones = RecordQuery(
        dataset="survey-2024",
        schema="sample",
        filter_tree={"field": "@open_notes", "op": "eq", "value": True},
    )
    print(project.note_svc.open_notes(open_ones).notes)

docs.title: Writing results back
docs.text:
• record_svc.add(collection, schema, data, parent_record_id=...) adds a record (inside another record when the schema is a child kind).
  • record_svc.patch(record_id, {"field": value}) changes only those fields and writes nothing when they already hold those values.
  • record_svc.update(record_id, data) replaces all of a record's data, so any field you leave out is cleared. Use patch unless that is what you want.

To attach a file, store it first and then put its reference in a file field:

from pathlib import Path

with civex.open() as project:
    survey = project.dataset_svc.get("survey-2024")
    ref = project.file_svc.store(Path("out/profile.png"), collection_id=str(survey.id))
    project.record_svc.patch(record_id, {"profile": ref.to_dict()})

Values are checked as they would be in the app. A value a field doesn't allow raises civex.domain.exceptions.ValidationError, and a name that doesn't exist raises NotFoundError.

docs.title: Automations
docs.text: Adding or changing a record queues any workflow whose trigger matches, just as an edit in the app does. The runs happen wherever automations are being run: the app (civex serve) runs them on its own, and without it civex automation run runs what's waiting.

docs.title: Alongside the app and the command line
docs.text: A script can work on a project while the app is open or a civex command is running. On SQLite, a write waits briefly for another one to finish. Keep each with block short in a long-running script, because the block holds its changes until it ends.

docs.title: What's there
docs.text:
The opened project has one service per area, for example:

Attribute For schema_svc Schemas and their fields dataset_svc Collections record_svc Records: find, summarise, points, add, patch, update, delete, restore, move file_svc Storing and reading files view_svc Saved views file_access_svc Exports of files and tables; frame and typed_rows history_svc History and revert bundle_svc Bundles for moving data between projects config The project's settings and its folder (config.project_root)

These are the methods the command line and the app call, and they are documented in their docstrings (help(project.record_svc.patch)).

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
A release is a frozen, citable copy of a project's data. A paper, a thesis or a data deposit can say exactly which data it used ("release v1, content hash sha256:4f1c…"), and that data can be had back later, however much the project has changed since.

Releases are published on a civex hub

A release made on a personal computer would be neither authentic nor reachable by anyone else, so a release is made, kept and shared by a host (a civex hub), and is never synced. Only a host switches it on (the releases feature); the app on your computer has no Releases pages, and civex release only says so: there is no command to create, list, read or export one here. A bundle (civex bundle export) is the free, local copy; a release is the hub's layer over it: a permanent name, frozen content, a citation, a public page and access control. To take a hub's release, use civex clone <repo-url> --release NAME (see below). Releases an older civex made on a computer are no longer shown there.

A release has:

  • a version you choose (v1, 2026-thesis): letters, digits, ., _ and -; it can't be changed later;
  • citation details: a title, a description, the authors in citation order (each with an ORCID and an affiliation if they have them), a licence (an SPDX id such as CC-BY-4.0, or any other), keywords and, if it has one, a DOI;
  • what it covers: the whole project, some collections, a saved list, or records chosen in the explorer (each with the records above it and everything inside it, so an encounter comes with its recordings and it reads back whole);
  • a small bundle of records: schemas, collections and records with their ids (and, only if you tick Include workflows and plugins, their code: it is left out by default, since code may not be yours to publish), plus a release.json manifest and a CITATION.cff;
  • the files its records cite, which it keeps where they are. Nothing is copied: the release becomes one more owner of each file, like the records that use it.

Because only the records are written, making a release of a project with terabytes of files across many drives takes moments, and needs none of those drives plugged in.

docs.title: Making one
docs.text:
civex's own app has no screen that makes a release: the host does (a civex hub has its own full-page wizard). In civex's records list, Release these… (on a host that mounts the app with an onRelease handler; otherwise it is not shown) hands the host the chosen records, or the query behind them, and the host takes it from there. The handler receives the JSON of the API's ReleaseScopeRequest: { "records": [ids] } for ticked records or { "query": {...} } for every match, and the query can select by created_after / created_before (ISO 8601; no offset means UTC) as well as by collection, kind (schema_name), filter, where and search.

A host written in Python builds the scope without private imports:

from civex.domain.release import ReleaseScope           # or
from civex.server.models import ReleaseScopeRequest

body = ReleaseScopeRequest.model_validate(scope_json)    # what onRelease gave
ctx.release_svc.create("v1", "Seal survey", scope=body.scope(),
                       include_workflows=body.include_workflows)

ctx.release_svc.plan(scope) counts what it would hold first. A host that does not use Python can call POST /releases/plan and POST /releases with the same JSON.

There is no command that makes one: civex release create was removed, and civex release says "Releases are published on a civex hub".

Making, correcting, withdrawing and yanking a release need the release permission (release). A role that could change the project's structure (change_structure) has it too, unless the host withholds it, so a self-hosted authority that enables the feature behaves as it did.

docs.title: The content hash
docs.text:
Each record in a release has a hash of its own: of its id, its collection, its kind, the record it sits inside and its values, with each value keyed by the field's id rather than its name. Renaming a field or changing its name on screen changes no record's hash. The release keeps these, sorted by record id, in records.hashes, beside structure.json (its schemas, fields and collections with their ids).

The content hash is a sha256 over what the release holds, not over the zip's bytes (a zip records the time it was written). It covers, in a fixed order: the structure, every record's hash (by record id), the sha256 of every file the records cite (sorted), and any workflows and plugins it was made with. A file is covered by its own hash, so no file is read to make or check it. Making a release of the same data again gives the same hash; changing one value, or the file a record cites, gives a different one.

docs.title: Its files
docs.text:
A release keeps every file its records cite, so a clean-up never removes one while the release exists, even after the records have let it go. A file's details (More details on a file, or civex store where) name the releases keeping it, and permanently deleting a record says which releases keep its files.

When files move between drives, a release goes with its records: emptying a drive moves everything on it, and gathering a collection onto another drive moves the release's copy too once every record using that copy has moved. A release never holds a copy back on its own; if some record still uses the copy where it was, the release stays with that one.

To get a release out, its page has one button, Export…, with the same two ways as any export:

  • Save to a folder: any folder of this computer (Choose…), with the files laid out as the records were (a folder per record). The folder also holds the release's records as one file, which Bring in from another project… (or civex bundle import) reads;
  • Download a zip: offered only while the release is small enough (2000 files, 500 MB).

Each folder and zip also holds manifest-sha256.txt (BagIt: each file's sha256 and its path), release.json and CITATION.cff, so it stands alone.

The page's menu has the two things that are not an export: Copy to another project… (the records alone, as one file) and Change storage drive… (which drive civex itself keeps the release's files on; only the release's own copies move).

docs.title: Checking a release
docs.text:
Verify (on the release's page) checks that:

  • the bundle's bytes still match the sha256 it is kept under;
  • every record's hash in records.hashes matches its record, hashed again;
  • the content hash, recomputed, is the one it was made with;
  • every file it cites is recorded on a drive here (on a computer that leaves files to the server, missing files are only noted).

It reads no file, so it is quick however large the release.

Read every file back (the deep check) also reads every file against its hash, with its progress in the status bar. A copy whose bytes don't match is reported and removed, as a clean-up's check does.

docs.title: Citing it
docs.text: The release's page has its citation as plain text, BibTeX and CITATION.cff, each with a copy button.

docs.title: What changed since
docs.text:
Changed since compares the release with the data now, record by record: each record it holds is hashed again as it is now and compared with its hash in the release. For each collection it counts the records:

  • added: in what the release covers now, and not in the release;
  • changed: in both, with a different value or in a different place;
  • removed: in the release, and deleted or permanently deleted since.

A record is in only one of these. An edit that was undone counts as unchanged, and every computer gives the same answer, since history is not read. Schemas and fields added, removed or changed since (a rename among them) are listed separately. Deleting a field since makes the records that held a value for it count as changed.

Each number opens the records it means; a changed record shows which fields differ, with the value in the release and the value now. A large release is compared in the background, with its progress in the status bar.

docs.title: Correcting, withdrawing and yanking
docs.text:
A release's content never changes. Its citation details can be corrected (a typo in the title, a DOI issued later: Edit details…).

It can be withdrawn with a reason (Withdraw…): it says so wherever it is shown, and keeps its data, so work that cited it can still be checked.

It can be yanked with a reason (Yank…) when its data must go. It stops keeping its files and its bundle, so the next clean-up removes whatever nothing else uses. You are told first how many files that is, and how many stay for the records that still use them. What is left is the release's record: its name, content hash, citation, and who yanked it, when and why, so a citation still finds it. A yank can't be undone.

Corrections, withdrawals and yanks are recorded in history.

docs.title: Getting the records back
docs.text:
A host serves each release as one bundle with its files (GET /releases/{name}/bundle, built on disk and streamed). Over plain HTTPS that is a download you read into a new project with civex bundle import; or let civex do both:

civex clone https://hub.example.org/ada/seals/data --release v1

This makes a new project from the release: nothing is joined or synced, and it starts read-only (a copy to read and cite; --writable allows changes). A private repository needs the host's token (--token, or CIVEX_TOKEN). Workflows and plugins in the bundle are not installed.

docs.title: On a project that syncs
docs.text: Releases are never synced (sync protocol 6). A device does not send them, the authority does not feed or snapshot them and refuses one it is sent (the refusal code is not_synced), and the files a release keeps are not something a device sends or fetches. The files a release keeps stay on the host that made it (it owns them in its catalogue, so they are never cleaned up while the release is not yanked).

docs.title: Record types & fields
docs.text: A record type is a blank form: the fields one kind of thing has, their types and the rules on each. The CLI and the API call it a schema. You design it once; every record of that type is one filled-in copy of the form, and lives in a collection. Types can go inside other types (a Site holds Visits, which hold Samples). New to these ideas? Start with Record types, collections and records.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
civex schema create site --label "Site"
civex schema add-field site name --type string --required
civex schema add-field site location --type geo

civex schema create visit --parent site --label "Visit"
civex schema add-field visit visited_on --type date --required --precision month
civex schema add-field visit team --type string

civex schema create sample --parent visit --label "Sample"
civex schema add-field sample number --type integer --min 1
civex schema add-field sample depth --type float --unit m --min 0
civex schema add-field sample taken_at --type datetime
civex schema add-field sample photo --type file --accept ".jpg,.png"
civex schema add-field sample reading --type file --accept ".csv"
civex schema update sample --display-template "Sample {number:02}"

civex schema show sample

Sample (sample)
  Inherits: visit
Label       Field       Type      Required  Source
Number      number      integer             sample
Depth       depth       float               sample
Taken At    taken_at    datetime            sample
Photo       photo       file                sample
Reading     reading     file                sample
Visited On  visited_on  date      yes       ↑ visit
Team        team        string              ↑ visit
Name        name        string    yes       ↑ site
Location    location    geo                 ↑ site

Three record types, designed once. From here on the project only gets records: sites, visits and samples.

In the app: Record types → New record type, then Add field on its page. Type the label and the name fills itself in. The rules offered depend on the kind of field you pick.

docs.title: Field types
docs.text: Type In the app Stores Typed as string Text One line of text North Ridge longtext Text box Several lines (newlines kept) integer Whole number 42 float Number Optionally in a fixed unit 3.14, 1024 ft boolean Yes/no yes, true, 1 / no, false, 0 date Date A day, or a month or year if allowed 2024-03-15, 2024-03, 2024 datetime Date and time A UTC instant, to the second 2024-03-15T09:30:00 geo Location A GeoJSON point, line or area 56.12, -3.41 file / file_list File / Files References to stored files a path reference / reference_list Link(s) to records Record ids an id or unique prefix tags Tags A list of short labels seal, tagged url Web address http(s):// text https://example.org enum Choice (legacy) Use string with --choices instead formula Formula Nothing: worked out from other fields when read (can't be typed in)

docs.title: Rules on a field
docs.text:
Rules are checked whenever a record is saved: in the app, the CLI, the API, imports and workflows.

Flag Types Example --required / --optional all --min / --max integer, float --min 0 --max 100 --choices string --choices "pass,fail,inconclusive" (a dropdown in the app) --max-length string, longtext --max-length 500 --unit float --unit m, --unit degC --precision date --precision month (accepts 2024-03 and 2024-03-15) --geometry-types geo --geometry-types Point,Polygon --bbox geo --bbox "-12,48,4,62" (west,south,east,north) --accept file, file_list --accept ".jpg,.png" --max-size file, file_list --max-size 10485760 (bytes) --references reference, reference_list --references species --from-file + --filename-pattern string, integer, float, date, datetime --from-file reading --filename-pattern "YYYYMMDD[-_]HHmmSS" (read from the file's name when the file is attached or replaced; see Fill fields from file names)

Changing a rule doesn't re-check the values already stored. Before you save, the field editor says how many records hold a value the new rules refuse (or leave a newly required field empty), names a few, and links to the data check that lists them all; civex schema update-field says the same and asks before going on (POST /api/schemas/{schema}/fields/{field}/check with the rules you would set). Those records keep their values and can still be edited: a save checks only the values it changes, so a broken value is refused only when it is changed to another one the rules refuse.

Some rules are set in the app (or over the API, as restrictions) only: a date/datetime minimum and maximum, a datetime field's own timezone, and a file's download-name template.

docs.title: Units
docs.text: A float with a unit stores every value in that unit. Conversion happens only as data comes in: typing 1024 ft into a metres field stores 312.1152, and the CSV import asks which unit each column is in. Changing a field's unit later relabels it and converts nothing, so to switch units add a new field. Units civex doesn't know (umol/kg) are plain labels.

docs.title: Partial dates
docs.text: --precision is the least precise value a date field accepts: year takes 2019, 2019-06 and 2019-06-14; month the last two; day (default) only full dates. Values are stored as written, never padded. Minimums and maximums compare whole periods, so 2020 fails a minimum of 2020-03.

docs.title: Times and timezones
docs.text:
A datetime is stored as a UTC instant. A value with an offset (2024-03-15T09:30:00-05:00) is exact. A value without one, from a CSV, an instrument or a file name, is read as wall time in the field's timezone, else the collection's, else UTC:

civex collection update survey-2024 --timezone Europe/London

Times that don't exist or happen twice at a DST change are rejected rather than guessed: add an offset. Changing a timezone changes how values are shown and how new ones are read, never what is stored.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
A geo field holds GeoJSON in WGS84 (longitude first). It reads the ways people write coordinates:

56.12, -3.41          56.12N 3.41W          56°07'12"N 3°24'36"W
N 56° 07.2' W 3° 24.6'                      POINT(-3.41 56.12)

Exports and CSVs write a point as lat, lon, and other shapes as GeoJSON. A point may carry uncertainty_m and an elevation (negative for depth). A --bbox with west greater than east crosses the 180th meridian.

On a record, Edit on map… places a point or draws a line or area, takes coordinates in any format, imports GeoJSON, GPX, KML or WKT, and changes nothing until Apply. The map works offline with built-in coastlines. For street detail, set a tile server in Settings → Map ([map] tile_url and attribution in config.toml), following that provider's terms.

docs.title: Names and labels
docs.text:
name label In the app Key, folded under the name with a change link Name Is the machine key the display name Looks like visited_on (lowercase, digits, _) Visited On (anything) Used by workflow YAML, CSV headers, templates, API paths the app, schema show, forms Changing it a real rename (see below) always safe

Without a label, one is derived from the name. Records store values by field id, so a rename never touches stored data, and templates are updated for you. Workflow YAML that names the old field must be updated by hand.

civex schema update-field sample number --label "Sample number"   # safe
civex schema update-field sample number --rename sample_no        # update workflows
civex schema lint                                                # names that aren't valid slugs

docs.title: Naming records and files
docs.text:
A record's name comes from its record type's template. It shows in lists, breadcrumbs, references and export folder names.

civex schema update sample --display-template "{species.common}-{taken_at:YYYY-MM}-{number:03}"
civex schema update sample --clear-display-template
Write Gives {team} the value {team:upper}, :lower, :title NORTH RIDGE, … {team:slug} north_ridge {team:trunc(3)} Nor {visited_on:YYYY-MM-DD} a date pattern (YYYY MM DD HH mm SS) {number:03}, {depth:.1f} 007, 12.5 {species.common} a field of the record the reference species points at {schema}, {id} the record type's name, the record's short id {{, }} literal braces
  • A blank value is dropped with the separator beside it: {team} - {number} with no team gives just 7.
  • The first nameable field you add becomes the template, so new record types name records from the start.
  • {ref.field} reaches one level through a single reference field that names its target schema. Editing the target renames at once.
  • Renaming or deleting a field updates every template that uses it.

A file field's download name (set on the field in the app) uses the same builder. It names the stem, keeps the file's own extension, and may use fields of records above and through any reference: {species.common}_{name}_{number:02}.

docs.title: Formulas
docs.text:
A formula field is worked out from the record's other fields each time the record is read: a duration, a ratio, a converted unit, a label made of two codes. Nothing is stored, so it never drifts from the values it reads and changing the formula changes every record at once, with no run to wait for.

civex schema add-field patient bmi --type formula --expression "mass / height ** 2" --decimals 1
civex schema add-field patient stay --type formula -e "days_between(admitted, discharged)" --result integer
civex schema add-field dive depth_m --type formula -e "depth_ft * 0.3048" --unit m
civex schema add-field sample code --type formula -e 'concat(site.code, "-", number)'
civex schema preview-formula patient "round(mass / height ** 2, 1)" --record 3f2a
Write Means mass, site.code a field of the record (or of a record above it), or a field of the record a link points at 12, 0.3048, "text", True a number, text, yes/no + - * / // % ** arithmetic (+ also joins two texts) == != < <= > >=, and or not comparisons and logic "deep" if depth > 200 else "shallow" a choice round(x, 2), abs, min, max, sqrt, log(x[, base]), exp, floor, ceil numbers concat(a, "-", b), str, upper, lower, len text (and len of tags) days_between(start, end), hours_between(start, end), year, month, day, date_add(date, days) dates and times coalesce(value, fallback) the first value that isn't blank
  • Blank in, blank out: a formula reading an empty field is empty, unless coalesce gives it something else.
  • What it gives (--result: float, integer, string, boolean, date, datetime) is worked out from the formula when you leave it out. A decimal result can have --decimals and a --unit, which tables and DataFrames carry.
  • A value that can't be worked out for one record (dividing by zero, a value of the wrong kind) is left blank there with the reason shown on the record; the rest of the list is unaffected.
  • The formula is checked when you save it: the fields must exist and fit, and formulas can't read each other in a circle. One formula can read another, and a field of a record above, including its formula. A link reaches only stored values of the record it points at.
  • Renaming a field rewrites the formulas that read it. A field a formula reads can't be deleted until the formula is changed or deleted.
  • A formula can't be required, have a default, be part of a record's name or a unique key, or be set by an edit, an import or a workflow (a value sent for it is ignored).
  • Lists can't be filtered, sorted or summarised by a formula: the database holds no value for it. Formulas do show as columns in the explorer and in exported tables, and in ctx.frame() / ctx.rows(), typed by what they give.
  • Over the API a record's formulas are in derived (never in data), with formula_errors saying why one is blank. History, sync and bundles hold no formula values; a bundle carries the formula itself.

In the app, the field editor's Formula box puts field names and functions in at the cursor and shows what the formula gives for the latest record of that kind, or one you pick.

docs.title: Types inside other types
docs.text:
civex schema create sample --parent visit

In the app this is Goes inside when you create the type. A record of a child type sits inside a record of the parent type: every sample is filed under its visit, and every visit under its site. A child stores only its own fields, but filters, sorts, columns and templates can use its parents' fields, and parents can be filtered by their children ("sites that have a sample where…"). The parent can't be changed after creation.

This is still three record types and many records. Don't make a record type per site: Site is the type, and North Ridge and East Shore are two records of it.

docs.title: Keeping records unique
docs.text:
civex schema add-unique sample number    # no two samples in a visit share a number
civex schema unique sample
civex schema remove-unique sample number

In the app: the record type's Uniqueness tab.

  • Checked among records of that type under the same parent (the samples of one visit), or for top-level records in the same collection.
  • A record with a blank in any of the rule's fields isn't held to it.
  • Only the type's own scalar fields (text, numbers, dates, yes/no, choices, links). Not files, locations, tags or lists.
  • You can't add a rule while records already break it. The message names clashing records.
  • A refused save names the record that already has the values. Workflow steps skip such rows and list them in a duplicates output.
  • A deleted record frees its values. Restoring it is refused if another record took them.

docs.title: Charts for a kind
docs.text:
A kind of record says which charts its lists open with, on its Charts tab: the same chart cards as beside any list of records (see Charts), drawn here over every record of the kind. Add, reorder or remove them, here or beside any list of the kind; each change is saved for everyone, is in the kind's history and syncs. A kind starts with no charts.

A chart follows a field that is renamed, and goes when a field it uses is deleted.

civex schema charts list sample
civex schema charts add sample --by site --measure mean:depth
civex schema charts add sample --by taken:month
civex schema charts add sample --map position --title "Where they are"
civex schema charts remove sample <id>
civex schema charts clear sample        # no charts again

The API is PUT /api/schemas/{schema}/charts with the whole list.

docs.title: Faster sorting and filtering: indexed fields
docs.text:
With hundreds of thousands of records of one type, sorting a list by a field, or counting the records a filter on it matches, can take seconds. An index on the field makes those fast (a sort's first page in a millisecond at a million records) and makes saving records of that type slightly slower.

civex schema index sample depth          # index it
civex schema index sample depth --off    # stop
civex db indexes                         # what is indexed, and built yet
civex db indexes --reconcile             # build what is missing now, showing progress

In the app: the field's settings, Indexed.

  • Fields in a uniqueness rule are always indexed (every save checks them).
  • Only single values can be indexed (text, numbers, dates, yes/no, choices, links), like a uniqueness rule. An inherited field is indexed on the type that defines it.
  • An index belongs to this computer's database: it is a setting in config.toml ([db] indexed_fields, by field id, so renaming a field keeps it), never synced or in the history. After moving the database (civex db move) the same indexes are built in the new one.
  • Indexes are always built and dropped in the background: by a running civex serve (the status bar shows "Speeding up sorting on …"), or by a process the command that changed them starts, so the command returns at once. Lists work meanwhile, only slower. civex db indexes --reconcile does it in front of you instead.
  • On a big table a build takes a while (a minute or two at a million records). On SQLite a build gives way whenever someone saves a record, and starts again once nobody has saved for a few seconds, so saving never waits for it; under constant saving an index waits for a pause.
  • Indexes help sorting and filtering inside a collection. Counting every record of a type, and text search, still read every record.

docs.title: Changing and deleting fields and types
docs.text:
civex schema update-field sample depth --min 0 --max 50     # merges with existing rules
civex schema update-field visit team --optional
civex schema update-field sample depth --clear-restrictions
civex schema remove-field sample depth
civex schema delete sample

A field's type can't change. Removing a field is reversible: records keep their values, shown under Deleted fields on the record, and restoring the field brings them back. Deleting a record type takes its records to Recently Deleted. See Deleting & restoring data.

docs.title: Server & web UI
docs.text: civex serve starts civex's web app and HTTP API for the project you're in. It runs on your own computer, for you, like git: there are no accounts or passwords.

docs.title: Start it
docs.text:
From inside a project (any folder at or below the one holding _civex/):

civex serve --open

This starts the server at http://localhost:8000 and opens it in your browser. Stop it with Ctrl+C.

To start it with a double-click instead, run civex shortcut once: it puts a shortcut for this project on your Desktop.

docs.title: Who can reach it
docs.text:
By default only this computer can. Pick the row that matches what you want:

You want… Do this To use civex yourself, on this computer civex serve (the default) Other computers to sync with this project civex serve --sync-only, reached over HTTPS: see Sync a project between computers To use this computer's civex from another computer Forward the port over SSH: ssh -L 8000:localhost:8000 <this computer>, then open http://localhost:8000 there

Sharing the web app itself on a network isn't supported: it has no sign-in, so anyone who could reach it could read and change everything, and run workflows. --allow-remote (below) exists for setups that put their own protection in front, and civex prints a warning when it's used.

What protects the default

The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only, so other computers can't connect at all. It also refuses requests that don't come from this computer's own pages: a Host header that isn't localhost (DNS rebinding) and a change sent from another site (Origin, cross-site request forgery).

docs.title: The web UI
docs.text:
The left-hand navigation has:

Section What it's for More Home Your pinned saved filters with live counts, and what you opened lately Collections Browse and edit records, their files and everything under them; search, filter, save views, export Collections & records, Views Exports Saved exports, and the folders they've made Exports Activity Every change, who made it, and restoring what was deleted Deleting & restoring Schemas The kinds of record, their fields and rules Schemas & fields Workflows, Runs Automations and each time one ran Workflows, Automation Settings Appearance, database, storage, retention, sync, map

A few things work everywhere:

  • Ctrl+K (⌘K on a Mac) jumps to any collection, schema, saved filter or record by name.
  • The star pins a collection, record, saved filter or place to the top of the navigation. Pins and recent items are kept in this browser only.
  • Shift-click a second tick box to tick everything between it and the last one you clicked.
  • The status bar at the bottom shows work going on in the background (file moves, workflow runs, sync) and anything that needs you.
  • Dates are shown and typed as DD/MM/YYYY unless you choose another pattern in Settings → Appearance → Date format: MM/DD/YYYY, YYYY-MM-DD or D MMM YYYY (14 Jun 2019). Times are 24-hour. A date field that takes a month or a year shows it the same way (06/2019, 2019). Every date box reads what you type in that pattern (an ISO date like 2019-06-14 works in any) and has a calendar button. The choice is kept in this browser only, and it changes only what you see: what is stored, the API, exported tables and the CLI keep YYYY-MM-DD.

docs.title: HTTP API
docs.text:
Everything the web UI does goes through /api/, as JSON. The full, current list of endpoints is at /docs while the server runs. Two you're likely to script against:

# Upload a file; use the returned sha256 as a file field's value
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/files -F "file=@20240315_093000.csv"
# → {"sha256": "abc123…", "filename": "20240315_093000.csv", "size": 4096000}

# Run a workflow against a record
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/api/workflows/extract-start-time/run \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"record_id": "abc123…"}'

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Default What it does --open off Open the browser once the server is up (or just open it, if civex is already running on that port) --port, -p 8000 The port to listen on --sync-only off Serve only what syncing devices call; see Syncing between machines --log-level INFO DEBUG, INFO, WARNING or ERROR; see Logging & telemetry --host 127.0.0.1 The address to listen on. Anything but this computer's own is refused without --allow-remote --allow-remote off Allow --host to be a network address. There is no sign-in: only behind protection of your own --reload off Restart when civex's own code changes, for working on civex itself

docs.title: Storage volumes
docs.text: Where civex keeps files, and how they move between drives. For the step-by-step version, see Put files on another drive.

docs.title: The object store
docs.text:
A file's bytes are stored once per drive, named by their SHA-256 hash, in the same layout as Git:

_civex/objects/
  3f/9c01ab…e2          ← the bytes of one file, no name or extension
  manifest.jsonl        ← {"sha256", "filename", "size"} per file, for humans

A record holds a small reference, {sha256, filename, size}. So:

  • The same content is stored once per drive, however many records use it.
  • Stored files never change. Editing means attaching a new file.
  • manifest.jsonl says what each blob originally was, so a bare copy of a volume is readable even without civex.

docs.title: Volumes
docs.text:
A volume is a folder that holds objects, usually on its own drive. Every project starts with default (_civex/objects). Volumes are defined in _civex/config.toml; the database only records which files are on which volume.

[store]
volume_queue = ["new-archive", "default"]

[store.volumes.new-archive]
path = "/media/new-archive/civex"
allocated_gb = 500.0
id = "6c1f…"            # matches the .civex-volume marker on the drive
Command Does civex store list Each volume's status, space and place in the queue civex store add <name> --path P [--allocated-gb N] [--queue] Add a folder as a volume civex store update <name> --path P The drive is now mounted somewhere else civex store queue A B … Order tried for new files with no home civex store set-state <name> active\|readonly\|retired Stop writing to it civex store adopt <name> "This is that drive" (marker lost or drive re-formatted) civex store remove <name> Forget it. Nothing on the drive is deleted

Identity. civex store add writes a .civex-volume marker into the folder.
